utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Registrar, may I ask you please to call the case on the Appeals Chamber's agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-95-13/1-R.1, the Prosecutor versus Veselin Sljivancanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. May I ask Mr. Sljivancanin if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I can hear you and I understand everything and I am capable of following the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. With me today, Ms. Najwa Nabti, Mr. Kyle Wood, and our case manager, Mr. Colin Nawrot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. Appearances for Mr. Sljivancanin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Sljivancanin is represented today in the courtroom by myself, Novak Lukic, I am his counsel from Belgrade; next to me is my co-counsel, Mr. Stephane Bourgon; and together with us in the courtroom we have our assistant, Caroline Bouchard; as well as our case manager, Mr. Boris Zorko; and with your approval, Mr. Landry, our military consultant is present with us here today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before we proceed, the Bench would like to issue an oral ruling with respect to the Prosecution's notice of filing addendum to Exhibit RP-7, the Theunens expert report, filed by the Prosecution on 11 October. Could counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin confirm whether they agree with this notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have received notice of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. So we have -- we'll then grant the Prosecution's request and direct the admission of the addendum annexed to the notice into evidence as part of exhibit RP-7. Now, turning to the main focus on the afternoon. This, as you know, is a Review Hearing in the case of the Prosecutor versus Veselin Sljivancanin. At the outset I will briefly summarise the issues which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. I will underscore again that none of my comments today expresses in any way the Appeals Chamber's views on the outcome of review proceedings. During this hearing, counsel will first examine the witness, Reynaud Theunens, and will then present summary arguments. I would underscore, the parties should provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments. I will now turn to the timetable for the proceedings. This hearing will proceed according to the schedule outlined in the decision on admission of evidence and Scheduling Order issued on 21 September 2010. The Prosecution will conduct the examination-in-chief of Mr. Theunens for one hour. Following a 20-minute pause, counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will cross-examine Mr. Theunens for one hour. The Prosecution will then conduct a re-examination of Mr. Theunens for 15 minutes. Following a 20-minute pause, the Prosecution and counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will each present summary arguments for 30 minutes in that order. I note the parties need not exhaust the entirety of their allotted time. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Having said that, I would now like to call witness Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Witness Theunens, could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. You may now be seated. Mr. Theunens, you are being asked to testify in conjunction with Mr. Sljivancanin's application for review of his conviction for aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. In the course of the afternoon, counsel for the Prosecution and Mr. -- and for Mr. Sljivancanin will both put questions to you concerning certain issues relating to his conviction. Judges may also choose to ask you questions. So I would now like to invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin the examination-in-chief. Ms. Brady, you are starting that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Firstly, good afternoon, Mr. Theunens. And as you know, my name is Helen Brady and I'll be asking you questions in examination-in-chief this afternoon. Before I start, just a few brief points. Firstly, we both speak English, so please remember to take a brief pause -- wait for a brief pause after my question before you answer so that the interpreters don't -- can follow. And secondly, as you already know, your report and CV have already been admitted in these proceedings, that's as Exhibits 7 and 8, and that includes the addendum to your report that you made yesterday, that's part of Exhibit 7. So with those things in mind, I would firstly like to ask you, Mr. Theunens, a few introductory questions, and again because your CV has already been admitted I won't spend too much time on this. But for the benefit of the record and the Bench, could you please provide just a summary background on your education and your work experience.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, after I graduated from military academy in Brussels with a master's degree end of 1987, I spent three years in a tank battalion in -- with the Belgian armed forces in Germany as a platoon commander, acting company commander, and personnel officer. After that I was called back to military academy to be an instructor. Subsequently I was transferred to the Ministry of Defence to work as an intelligence analyst on Balkans, Ministry of Defence of Belgium, obviously. During that time-period which covered more or less nine years, I was also deployed three times in peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia. I mean, the details you can find in my CV. At the end of those nine years, I also worked in plans and policy, again at the Ministry of Defence, intelligence plans and policy. Then in 2001, in July -- excuse me, in June 2001 I moved to the ICTY, Office of the Prosecutor, where I worked until April last year as an intelligence analyst in the military analysis team. I've -- my work mainly consisted of cases involving Serb perpetrators, i.e., JNA, volunteers, and Territorial Defence. And then last year in April I left the ICTY to move to southern Lebanon to UNIFIL where I work since then as a chief of a joint mission analysis centre. And just to be coherent, I mean it's also in the CV, I attended specialised intelligence training in the UK and the US.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my friend is standing up. Perhaps he wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'd just like to know -- I see that the witness has some material in front of him. I'd just like to know what the material is before we go on. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a binder with a printed version of my CV and a printed version of my report which I annotated myself in order to again find back the important points. I mean, if you want I can remove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I can see no problem with that, and I'm sure you can't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what it was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It was a legitimate question. I see no problem, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: You said that you worked at the ICTY between 2001 and 2009, last year, as a military analyst in the military analyst team of the OTP. In that regard you prepared expert reports for the purpose of court proceedings and you testified for the Prosecution in several cases. Could you tell us about these cases, these reports.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I -- Your Honours, I testified in five trials. The first one was the trial of Slobodan Milosevic; second was the trial of Milan Martic; then there was the trial of Mile Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and Miroslav Radic; the fourth one was Vojislav Seselj; and the last one before I left was the trial of Ante Gotovina and Cermak and Markac. I plan to testify also in the trial of Radovan Karadzic and prior to that the trial of Frenki Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic. And so for these trials reports have been filed and admitted, I mean, except for the two last ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And in your time as a military analyst in the OTP, did you have occasion to analyse or study JNA military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Obviously because of the work I did prior to joining the MAT in the OTP, I was already familiar to a large extent SFRY military forces doctrine, JNA and Territorial Defence, as well as the doctrine and the activities of the different parties that participated in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1995. In addition, obviously here we had original documents, not only regulations but also orders, where we could see where it was actually, as an analyst, very interesting to see how the doctrine, i.e., the theory, was being implemented during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And coming to the report that's been admitted in these proceedings, Exhibit 7, can you tell us -- well, as background, you were asked by us, the Prosecution, to prepare a report in this case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And can you tell us the means by which you prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The documents I had access to I received -- or the documents I received from the appeals section are identified in the introduction of the report, and obviously I could also -- I remembered the report I drafted for this -- for the trial, and obviously I could also rely on the other knowledge and experience I still had of the various doctrinal issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And when were you contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor for that report and when did you come to The Hague in relation to that report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I received an e-mail in I think the second or the third week of July this year, and by coincidence I was in Belgium on rest and recreation annual leave and for a number of reasons I had no particular plans and since my residence is two hours away from here I replied that I was available, and then I spent I believe it was more or less a week here to prepare a preliminary report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And did you come back at another stage?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed. In the second half of August I was called back -- I mean UNIFIL put me -- how would I say? - provided me on loan to work approximately ten days here at the ICTY, not only for this case but also to review material for the Stanisic/Simatovic trial, as well as the Karadzic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And when you prepared your report what were you told was to be the scope of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in July I was basically told to have a look at the testimony of Mr. Panic and to, yeah, to draw analytical conclusions based on that testimony without precise questions. However, in August I received a number of questions, seven questions, from the appeals section of the OTP which I tried to answer to the best of my abilities in the report that I -- we have now in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And those questions are contained in the annex to your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now to the substance of your report, and the first thing I'd like to do, Mr. Theunens, is to show you an exhibit from trial. This is Exhibit 368. And I hope that -- it should be appearing on the screens in front of Your Honours in both English and B/C/S. Okay. I think we've got it. Do you see that, Mr. Theunens, on your screen now, it's Exhibit 368 from the Mrksic trial?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this document is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we can see from the title which is just beneath the left top heading, it's a regular combat report, "regular" stands for that it's produced at a regular time. I remember from working on this case that these reports were always dated at the end of the day, 1800. And so it covers the activities of the past 24 hours, i.e., this one would cover the activities of the time-period starting the 20th at 1800 until the 21st at 1800. And it's sent by -- as we can see the left, top heading, by this Operations Group South or south operative group command. And it discusses the activities, it starts with the enemy forces which are here called Ustasha forces, and the second paragraph, I'm sorry, discusses the activities of the friendly or the own forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And you've said who it comes from. Can you tell us who it is going to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. It's sent to two addressees. First of all, the command of the 1st Military District. Obviously because that's the superior command of Operational Group South in eastern Slavonia, and it's also sent to the secretariat of the -- I'm sorry, to the SSNO, so the secretariat for national or for people's defence. And why is that? Because the Guards Motorised Brigade, which is the main unit in Operative Group South, in peace time and prior to 30th of September, 1991, was subordinated to the SSNO through his chief of cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw your attention ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Why didn't you submit it with the other exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is already in the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I realise that, but still it would have made it easier for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: My apologies. I was under the impression that because it was a trial exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not suggesting that this is not correct, but still it would have made sense to add it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It probably would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention, Mr. Theunens, to the bottom of that exhibit, if you look at the B/C/S version of the exhibit you'll see a signature on that exhibit. What does that signature tell you about Mr. Panic's role on the 21st of November, according to JNA doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, as I have mentioned in my report, I believe it's on page 14 or one of these pages -- sorry, when I discuss reporting in the role of the commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic signs there as the commander or the acting commander of Operational Group South, and by signing he approves the contents of the document and he takes responsibility for it. And I have explained it in my report what the basis is for my conclusions on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And what position does it show him to be in that day?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I only -- I see only the B/C/S, but it's pretty obvious, it says "komandant OG JUG," so it means commander Operational Group South. Of course, the text is still the original one. It still says Mile Mrksic, but we know from other documents that were admitted in the trial and there is, for example, the resubordination order from the 21st in the morning which was also signed by Lieutenant Colonel Panic as acting commander, and this is the same signature. So it shows that at that moment in time Lieutenant Colonel Panic is the acting commander of Operational Group South.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Theunens, in your report --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is in his report in answer to question number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- you speak, Mr. Theunens, about the doctrine of single authority. Can you tell us briefly what this principle means?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Single authority is one of the three principles in the SFRY armed forces doctrine on command and control as they are stipulated in the All People's Defence law from 1982. In addition to single authority, there is also unity in command and obligation to implement decisions. And single authority means two things. It means, first, that there is only one commander at a time who is entitled to issue orders; and at the same time, there's only one person to whom the subordinate reports on the implementation of the order he or she has received from that commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And if you could also enlighten us, why is that doctrine or principle of single authority so important for -- under military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, obviously there can only be one commander at a time because otherwise there's confusion or even chaos. If two different people can issue orders at the same time to the same unit or to the same subordinate, the unit -- or I mean the subordinate unit or the subordinate person will be confused about what to do when and how. So that's why there's only one -- there can only be one commander at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: In light of that principle of single authority and bearing in mind Exhibit 368, in your opinion, and bearing in mind military doctrine, could Mrksic have exercised command authority over OG South during his absence? So that is the period when he was away from -- on the 21st to the 22nd of November?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Unless he would have violated a basic principle of command and control - and I have not seen any indication whatsoever about that during all the years I worked on this case, including requesting documents from the Republic of Serbia at the time - so unless he would have really violated that basic principle, it can be excluded that he, i.e., Mrksic, during his absence had any command authority over OG South.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, does that mean then that the signatory of Exhibit 368 had full command powers at the time he signed it over OG South?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: If you could look again at that exhibit, 368, the situational report that's on the screen, and you're familiar with it already from trial, does it include information about the status of the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: If we could go down on the -- to the bottom of the English part, please. Thank you. Well, we can see it talks about civilians who have been evacuated on the 20th and the 21st, including wounded. If we could move to the -- maybe the next English page just to be -- okay, it talks about the same activities that are conducted in relation to civilians and wounded. But there's no -- no mention is made of any activities in relation to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And from your knowledge of JNA doctrine and the circumstances of this case that you're familiar with, would you expect a situational report like this, like Exhibit 368, to have included information about prisoners of war; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I would have expected information on any activities with the prisoners of war and for two reasons. First of all, because we know from the context - and I have tried to summarise that in the report - the evacuation of Vukovar Hospital was what could be defined as a high-profile operation. Why? Because there was a specific agreement with the Croats which was -- I mean whereby the evacuation had to be supervised one way or the other by international observers. There was also a high interest from the security administration, including security organs who wanted to have as many prisoners of war as possible under JNA control in order to exchange them with prisoners the Croatian forces were holding. And at the same time we know, again from the context, that what happened with the evacuees from the hospital was not in accordance with the earlier instructions, be it written orders as well as what I just mentioned, the instructions given by the security administration, i.e., instead of bringing as many prisoners as possible to Serbia, Sremska Mitrovica, they were handed over to a body that was qualified as the local government and to the volunteers. And again for all those reasons, the high profile and the fact that the -- I mean, that the hand-over -- what did not correspond with the initial instructions received from the superior commands, those are key reasons to include that activity in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, in your report - and this is specifically in answer to the question that we asked you, question number 5, in that report you speak of a principle known as the duty of situational awareness. Can you tell us what this principle means.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be fully precise, I'm not the sure whether the word or the expression situational awareness as such is used in SFRY armed forces doctrine, but when you talk about, for example, and that's on paragraph 2 of page 18 of my report about the function -- I mean the number of functions of command and control are defined. There is the function of organisation. Further on -- I mean, there are many JNA as well as SFRY armed forces regulations that clearly specify or clearly stipulate that the commander has to be familiar with the situation, not only of the enemy forces but also his own forces. And if you want I can explain why that is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's pretty obvious. In a sense a commander receives a mission from his superior. And in order to implement that mission, I mean talking here about combat operations, he will have to use his own forces to carry those orders out. Now, if he's not familiar with the status from his own forces, it is difficult to give orders to them. Because, for example, imagine that we are in an offensive scenario and okay in this situation OG South receives a task to capture a particular town before a particular time. It may be that a number of units of OG South are weaker or maybe one unit is less experienced and another unit has suffered a lot of losses, well, these are all factors -- or maybe one unit is less trained. These are all factors the commander has to take into account in order when he plans the -- he prepares the order for his subordinate units to make sure that he uses the best-qualified unit in order to achieve the task he has received in the most efficient and the most successful manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And if I could just interrupt you at that point, and when we're talking about this duty the commander has to be familiar with the situation at all times, I refer to it as shorthand as situational awareness, but when we're talking about that we're not just talking about in the actual heat of battle, are we?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, it is at all times the -- the regulations I have seen are very specific -- I mean, they put more emphasis for combat operations for obvious reasons, because then -- that is called the tempo of operations is much higher. But -- I mean if -- I didn't address that, but, for example, if you have to organise a parade you're not going to use, for example, a unit -- I mean, fresh recruits, so you will maybe use a unit -- forces that are better trained or have more experienced in parades and that is also part of situational awareness and maybe a bit of a less important situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: So even on the facts of this case, after the fall of Vukovar, after the combat was over, the commander or the acting commander as the case may be would have to take active steps to find out in accordance with that principle, or duty of situational awareness, to find out what's going on with the units who are in his chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, if I take you back again or remind you of Exhibit 368, under JNA doctrine by signing Exhibit 368, what then does that imply about the steps that the commander of OG South or the acting commander of OG South had taken?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, my signing the report he confirms that the report is accurate and complete. And again, the need, I mean, for that is pretty obvious. The superior command is -- has the same obligation of situational awareness, and the reporting you receive from subordinates is one of your sources in order to familiarise yourself with the status of your own forces. Another way would be to conduct inspections, like to visit a unit to see whether what they are saying is correct and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: So just taking your answer, when you say he had to ensure that the information is complete, how does he do that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, usually there is a reporting system whereby the subordinate units send reports to the superior units, and at the start of operations arrangements are made to ensure that the information is made available by the subordinate units at the appropriate times so that the superior command has sufficient time to compile the report. I'm talking there about regular reporting. Of course there can also be I would call irregular reporting, i.e., in case of emergency or a significant development. Because again, it's not a static situation even after the end -- after the fall of Vukovar, things are still happening, I mean, units are moving, units are preparing to withdraw. This is ongoing on a permanent basis and again it's described in the report, but the OG South will have an operational centre where all this information comes in by radio, by reporting, by liaison officers, by different means, and all that information is put together. People -- I mean, they can also keep a war diary. And then a selection is made of the relevant information that is then included in the regular combat report which is then forwarded to the superior command. Of course, at any time an irregular report can be sent. In addition - and I'm sorry for being so extensive - but in addition to relying on the reporting from the lower level, as I mentioned the superior command can implement the inspection function of command and control which is very logical. It means that you verify the degree of implementation of your instructions and also, if needed, if the degree of implementation does not correspond with the expectations that you take corrective action. Another way to ensure this information sharing are the briefings, there are regular briefings, I think they were also around 1800 or just after the report. I'm not sure anymore. There can be visits. I mean, there's so many ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And when you say that he had to, in signing that report, make sure he was fully informed, what would he do if reports were not forthcoming? What steps should that person take? You've mainly spoken about when reports are coming, but what if there are no reports coming his way, what's he obliged to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, then he will instruct the people in the operations centre or the people in the staff to ask the subordinate unit why there is no report. I mean, there can be many reasons. In the worst case if there is a breakdown of the communications system he can send somebody to collect the report or he can ask the subordinate unit to send a liaison officer with the information. Yeah, and again he can also conduct inspections, as I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say then that that duty to remain situationally aware would be an active duty to take steps if the information was not forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Of course, and it's what I tried to explain, the report -- it's also out of self-interest. If you have to organise an operation as a commander, and we know from the doctrine that you are responsible, you have all interest in having as much and as accurate information as possible because you don't want to be surprised in this scaling by your own forces in the specific case we are looking at because that is -- it should be one of the factors you can control. What the enemy will do -- or other factors. I mean, for example, the weather can suddenly create problems. These are things you don't control. And as a commander, and that's -- again I mention that in paragraph 8, the duty or the capacity to foresee. It's expected from a commander in SFRY armed forces that he is able to foresee events - and the reasons I explained in my report - the attitude -- I mean, the capabilities, the possibilities of your own subordinate forces is something that should be the least of a worry for yourself in order to get accurate information. I mean, it's important to have that information, but it should be the least difficult to obtain that information, again in a scenario as we had in OG South at the time of the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, you know because you've read the testimony of Mr. Panic that he testified that on the 21st of November he was basically preoccupied and attending to various tasks, organising a press conference, attending to the return of the Guards Brigade to Belgrade and to the transport of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: For Your Honours' benefit that's at the pre-review hearing transcript page 63 and 83.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Under JNA doctrine would such tasks that he's described affect his duty as a commander that day, on the 21st of November, especially that duty to remain situationally aware or to be familiar with the situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, not at all. Again, in all the years I worked here and also before and studying SFRY armed forces doctrine, workload is not a reason to reduce or not an excuse to reduce responsibility. I mean, again I think it's on page 8, it's clearly stated in JNA command and control doctrine or SFRY armed forces command and control doctrine, a commander, he can delegate authority for obvious reasons. I mean the -- otherwise the chief of Main Staff would have to talk to each and every individual soldier which doesn't work. So the commander can delegate authority but he cannot delegate responsibility. And by delegating authority he still remains responsible, obviously for the tasks he has delegated. And in this particular case, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was not alone on the 21st of November. He has the OG South. There is specialised personnel in the different branches who should be able to help him with planning and organising all these activities. And then it's his judgement call. And again, referring to the testimony -- I understand from the testimony that on the 20th of November, in the afternoon and the evening, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was very concerned about the situation of the evacuees or the prisoners of war at Ovcara and at that his Chief of Staff -- so he has no legal obligation to be interested. He is interested. Why? Because he is the chief of staff. And therefore I found it surprising, and I mentioned that in my report, that on the day when he is legally responsible, because he is the acting commander, he based on his testimony does not show any interest in the situation of the prisoners, and that's something I tried to highlight in my report. Based on my understanding of SFRY armed forces doctrine, that is unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Just taking you one step further then on the answer you've given, if a commander or acting commander is aware that he's got prisoners of war in his zone of responsibility, in your opinion would it be more important for him to be satisfied about the safety of those prisoners or would it be more important for him to attend to his other tasks such as preparing for press conferences and the return of the Guards four days later?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's not exclusive -- I mean, the fact that there are prisoners of war in the zone of responsibility means that it's a task for the -- for OG South. Now, he can take care of it himself or he can delegate it to somebody. It would make sense to delegate that responsibility over the situation of these prisoners of war, i.e., that they are handed over to the appropriate authority, that they are treated well, that nobody can escape, and so on, to another officer who he, i.e., Panic, thinks is qualified to carry out that task in the best possible manner. And that officer would then of course have to inform Panic about the way how he has implemented that order. He would also have to inform Panic about any problems he would encounter while carrying out that authority that Panic has delegated to him. But again, in coherence -- or in accordance, I'm sorry, with the doctrine, Panic would still remain responsible for the situation of the prisoners of war. And coming back to what I said earlier, taking into account the information he had on the 20th, the concern he showed on the 20th, it would seem logical that he would still show the same -- he would -- it would certainly seem logical that he would still show the same concern on 21st because on that day he is the acting commander and according to SFRY armed forces doctrine he is legally responsible for the activities and the -- the activities of his units and the situation in his zone of responsibility, including the situation of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to a slightly different topic which is also addressed in your report, and this is about the subordination of the 80th Motorised Brigade to the OG South. In your report - and this is the topic of your answer to our question number 2 - in your report you say that the 80th Motorised Brigade was subordinated to the OG South until at least the 23rd of November, 1991. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I say that because we have -- there is one order -- I mean, there's an order and there's also an OG South -- a regular combat report that still mention the 80th Motorised Brigade, and I discuss that on pages 9 and 10 of my report. I'm trying to locate the exhibit number of the order -- I know it's the order -- sorry, the order Colonel Mrksic gives on the 22nd which I think is Exhibit 424, where he instructs that as of the 23rd of November, 1991, the 80th Motorised Brigade is obliged, and so on. This is page 9 of my report. Now, if you're not -- I mean, you can only issue orders to units that are subordinated to you. And again we have to look at the context and I discuss the context in the report. So that's why I conclude in addition to the regular combat report of the 23rd that 80th Motorised Brigade has to remain or is still subordinated to OG South until at least the 23rd, 1800 -- the 23rd of November, 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And bearing in mind then that the transfer of subordination -- sorry. Let me start again. Bearing in mind that the transfer from OG South to the 80th Motorised Brigade occurred sometime -- well, between -- after 6.00 p.m. on the 23rd of November, prior to the 24th of November when the Guards left, can you tell us about the situation in between when preparations are going on for them -- for the Guards to depart.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is a clear example of the implementation or the principle of single authority, i.e., there's only one commander at a time. However, the hand-over is a process because it involves the movement of units -- I mean, one unit will replace the other, one command will replace the other. It also involves an exchange of information and that can take several days. But it's only at the time when there's the formal hand-over from one commander, I mean the previous commander to the new commander, that the actual hand-over takes place in the sense of command and control. So even if prior to that the units -- I mean, the 80th Brigade, there may be officers physically present at the OG South Command and they are meeting -- I mean, the plans are co-ordinated, the actual hand-over -- based on the fact that Colonel Mrksic still signs as the commander of OG South on the 23rd at 1800 -- and we don't have a regular combat report for the 24th with his signature, that's why I conclude that the hand-over -- the formal hand-over can only have taken place after the 23rd of November at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn now to my last set of questions, my last topic of questions. Most of your testimony that we've heard this afternoon has been about Panic's duties as acting commander on the 21st of November. As you know, the night before, on the 20th of November, Mr. Panic was in his usual role as Chief of Staff. All these duties that you've talked about this afternoon, especially the duty of situational awareness, can you tell us how they apply to the Chief of Staff, bearing in mind the role of a Chief of Staff. You touched a little bit already on this in answer, I know.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is largely discussed in the reply I provide to question 1 in a sense that the Chief of Staff, he -- basically he manages the staff. Now, it's maybe -- it's important to notice that in the JNA there was -- in addition to the staff you have a number of assistant commanders. So you have the commander at the top, under him the Chief of Staff who manages the staff; but in addition you also have three assistant commanders, especially in the Guards Motorised Brigade as well as OG South. These were the assistant commander for security, the assistant commander for logistics, and then the assistant commander for political guidance. And they have a direct relation with the commander. All the other staff officers, they are, as I said, managed by Chief of Staff. And just to summarise his role, the commander receives an assignment from his superior - in this case Colonel Mrksic would receive a task from the command of the 1st Military District, General Zivota Panic at the time. And then Mrksic consults with his Chief of Staff in order to transform that instruction which can be very short, can be very long, depends on the situation, into orders -- sorry, into instructions for the subordinate units. And each staff section will compile its part of the report -- of the -- excuse me, of the order. And -- so the Chief of Staff is the closest -- I would say closest collaborator of the commander because he's his interlocutor with the staff, and that's also what I tried to explain. There is no legal duty on the Chief of Staff to be aware of the situation, but he would be a very poor Chief of Staff if he, as the closest advisor to the commander, is not able to assure that he provides the most accurate and most complete information to his commander. Because that's actually also the duty of the staff in addition to elaborating orders and so on, it's -- the duty's also to ensure the situational awareness. So he has all interest in being aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, as we also know - and this is my last question - as we also know, Mr. Panic did become the acting commander the next day. Upon learning -- and that would have had to have been sometime before Mrksic left. Upon learning that he would be the acting commander the following day, under military doctrine what questions would we expect someone in the position of Mr. Panic, who was Chief of Staff at the time, about to take-over the role of acting commander, what should he be asking himself and his commander who is leaving, Mile Mrksic, in order to meet the duty he's about to assume to be aware of what's going on in all the units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is covered by the aspect of -- by the function of continuity of command and control which I have not addressed in this report, but it's in part 1 of my report that was admitted in the trial. But again -- obviously, Panic, as he will be held responsible for everything he does as the commander when Mrksic isn't there, he needs to ensure that Mrksic has given him all the information he, Panic, needs in order to successfully carry out the command over OG South. That doesn't -- that does not just include the instructions Mrksic has received from his superiors, but Panic would also have to know all the concerns Mrksic has in relation to the situation, what the enemy can do, what the problems are for -- eventual problems for friendly units, and so on. We discussed the issues of prisoners of war, he would have to -- he would need to have that information too. And if he doesn't receive it from Mrksic spontaneously, he would ask for it because he wants to be in the best position in order to ensure his responsibilities - when I say "he," I mean Panic - in order to ensure his responsibilities as commander or acting commander -- acting commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, that's all the questions that I have for Mr. Theunens in his examination-in-chief. Having said that, the Prosecution relies on the entirety of his evidence which has been admitted in the report that he's given, Exhibit Number 7. Today the questions were to highlight the salient features, but we rely on the whole of his report as well as his testimony that he's given this afternoon. I don't know whether Your Honours have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have one or two, and thank you very much for your testimony, Mr. Theunens. You state at page 4, paragraph 6, of your report that a commander can issue orders related to operations directly to his subordinate commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but that's not the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He can -- I mean, if he issues an order, for example, in writing, he will sign it. But that order -- that's what I tried to explain, the order that the commander gives for the kind of activities we are talking about will be based on, again -- on the work of the staff as I tried to explain. That's the command process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, I understand. Let me come then to the end of my question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I understand that this is your view, if I cite you, that it would have been "highly unusual" for Mr. Mrksic to issue the withdrawal order directly to the 80th Motorised Brigade without involving his Chief of Staff. And here is my question to you: Can you say that it is impossible, in contrast to highly unusual, that this is what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would say that since it includes human beings, nothing is impossible. I mean, theoretically, Mrksic could have done it, but the whole question is: Why? Because it would be -- yeah, a violation of the doctrine. It would be -- it would create a very difficult relations in his staff because everybody would wonder like: Why don't you inform us? Because even if we look at just the withdrawal of the MPs, this has an impact on the forces of OG South because these MPs become available for another unit. And again, you cannot issue an order in isolation because the effects will be visible on the ground. Even if he would -- I mean, imagine that he says directly to Vojnovic, but I wrote here that Ovcara was 10 kilometres away from Negoslavci, but I think it's much less but I didn't have a map at the time. Everybody would notice that suddenly the MPs are not there anymore, and maybe they wouldn't notice in a minute, but they would notice at the latest the next day because again the duty of situational awareness applies. And everybody would wonder like: Why are they gone? Why has Mrksic not told us? So again I think we would end up in the realm of conspiracy theories, and I haven't seen any justification for such -- that would justify such a conspiracy theory. Also mentioning that not just Vojnovic but also as I -- addressing paragraph 9, that Captain Karanfilov of the security organs, he was also informed of the order. So there are at least two people informed of the order; there is Colonel Vojnovic and there is Captain Karanfilov, who was a security organ in OG South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do you have any theory as to how the captain was informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explain, Your Honours, in paragraph 9 that as I mentioned earlier since the security organs have a direct relation with the commander because the chief of the security organs, he's an assistant commander for security, one cannot rule out that Mrksic would have spoken directly to the security organs, but then it would be highly unusual to - again looking at the context - that he would talk to a captain, whereas there is a deputy commander of the security organs Vukasinovic, and there is the chief -- I'm sorry, the commander of the chief of security organs, Sljivancanin, who Mrksic himself had put responsible for the evacuation operation. Again, it would be highly -- I mean, I wrote it, it would be a violation of the principles of command and control for the commander to jump -- I mean, to ignore the person he had appointed to lead the operation, to ignore the deputy of that person, and then to go directly to a kind of a junior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens, you explained it very well, but you still did not reach the conclusion that such a course of action would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I find it's very difficult to use the word "impossible" Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, you know the fog of war and things happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have one more question to you. Page 8, paragraph 2 -- 3 of your report, you state as follows: "Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic testified during the pre-review hearing on 3rd of June, 2010, that it was the 80th Motorised Brigade and not Operation Group South that was responsible for Ovcara." I had some difficulty in finding this statement exactly in his testimony. Could you direct us, either now or later, to this specific cite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- it was more like a conclusion I drew from his testimony which follows where I say like -- I mean where I quote Panic. "There was a different unit assuming responsibility." And at the end, I mean, footnote 46, "We did not have responsibility over that area anymore." So my conclusion was that Panic basically said that actually the 80th Brigade is responsible for Ovcara. I mean, that's my military interpretation of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: He did not explicitly say so, sir, that in fact OG South did not have authority over Ovcara at the relevant time? I see Ms. Brady may --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- enlighten the situation to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can, Your Honours. Essentially if -- and if you can see it in the instructions that we gave to our expert where we quoted certain portions of Panic's evidence. In particular, if you look at under that question 2 we exert -- it's on page 3 of our instructions when he provided the report. We've quoted two paragraphs of evidence of Mr. Panic at the pre-review hearing. One's at page 71 to 72 and the other was 83/84. Now, it is an interesting evolution of Panic's use of verb tenses, is very interesting if you look closely at how he describes the situation. He's talking about the 80th was going to take over, the 80th would take over, that's all true. But take a close look at these paragraphs that I've pointed you to, and there he's, in our submission, creating or implying or saying explicitly that the OG South did not have responsibility over that area anymore. Perhaps actually if it's easier I will quote directly from what he said. At -- okay, here -- at page 71 to 72 of the review transcript he said: "The commander of the 80th Brigade had taken charge of the area or taken over the command of the area. The Guards was preparing to go back to the Belgrade garrison. We did not have responsibility over that area anymore." And again, later in cross-examination at page 83 to 84, he said this: "On the 21st of November, 1991, the area of responsibility that includes Ovcara and the hangar where these suspects were was under the responsibility of the 80th Brigade, that is to say it was the 80th Brigade that had this area of responsibility that included Ovcara, and they had already taken over the area of responsibility that had previously been held by the Guards Brigade. Let me note that they had had that zone or area earlier on as well." So, Your Honours, it is a clear impression being made to this Chamber that it had already happened, the transfer had already happened. That's just not the case. We know that already from the Trial Chamber's findings, paragraphs 82 and 253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: You state then you were asked to prepare -- to submit your analytical conclusions and you did analytical conclusions which contains a different matter. So in the light of this conclusion let us -- if the report still -- although we had before us the report, Panic still credible in the light of the context of this report concerning Mrksic and Sljivancanin's conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it's up to me to say whether a witness is credible or not. What I have tried to do is to look at the testimony Mr. Panic has given, and I compared it with the SFRY armed forces or JNA military doctrine and I compared it with the other evidence that had been presented in the trial as well as the Trial Chamber's judgement and the Appeals Chamber judgement. And that's how I came to the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: I would ask your personal point of view on this point and thank you very much for the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Guney. And now my colleagues? So I think that we are I think ten minutes ahead of time, but we might still have now to proceed our 20-minute break. So we will resume at, shall we say I will be generous, at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bourgon rose to speak for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will be conducting the cross-examination of course on behalf of the applicant, Mr. Sljivancanin. I do not have too many questions for you. I hope to complete my cross in the time allotted, that is no more than one hour. Now, that being said, if there are any questions that you do not understand, a standard warning, you know the drill. Do not hesitate to tell me and I will repeat the question. Let me begin by introducing the people who are present with me today, simply because you weren't there when the introductions were made. Lead counsel in this case, Mr. Novak Lukic; Mr. Boris Zorko, case manager to my left; to my immediate left, Ms. Caroline Bouchard-Lauzon; and to my right the military expert that we have been working with, Lieutenant-Colonel, retired, Remi Landry, from Canada. Sir, I have three preliminary questions before I move into the substance of my cross-examination. And my first such preliminary question relates to your general military knowledge, having been a member of the Belgian armed forces for a number of years. And my question is straightforward. If a commander hears that a subordinate was convicted of a crime on the basis of information he knows is not true, would you expect this commander to come forward and provide the information in his possession in order to avoid an injustice?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, he should step forward. I would just be surprised why -- I mean, if he's in a position to give information and he's a commander, I would have expected that he -- the information that he has would also be available during the investigation phase, i.e., before that the conviction was pronounced. But okay, for one or the other reason that was not possible, yeah, he can always step forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, no, that's not my question. It's not he can always. Would you expect the reasonable commander to do so. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't think that -- I don't think that that is part of military doctrine. I mean, I haven't seen any regulations to that effect. I'm familiar with the procedure for the enforcement of military discipline and military justice in the JNA. As you know, the 1988 regulations --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, but let me answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, sir, that's not my question. I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As you stand here today before this courtroom as a member of the Belgian armed forces, are you saying that a commander from the Belgian armed forces who hears that a subordinate has done -- is being convicted on the basis of information he knows not to be true, will the information that this Belgian commander has, will he step forward, do you expect him to step forward or is it that Belgian commanders do not step forward and stay home with the information that they have? That's my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't think there's a reason to raise your voice. Secondly, I'm not here to testify about the Belgian armed forces. I'm here to testify about the SFRY armed forces. I wanted to explain, and I think it would be helpful for everybody to hear, that the 1988 regulations on the implementation of the laws of armed conflict by the SFRY armed forces say that any officer who has information that can be relevant for a crime has to make sure that the competent authorities have that information. And obviously that would happen during the investigation phase. Now, again, if that hasn't happened, then afterwards he has the right to do so and it would be more a moral issue I would say than a legal obligation. I haven't seen any reference to a legal obligation except during the investigation phase. But afterwards, yeah, I mean justice has to prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You're avoiding my question, but I will move on to my next. The second question relates to the Trial Chamber's judgement. The Trial Chamber's judgement adopted a number of findings in relation to the events which took place at Ovcara, including what happened at the Operational Group South Command and the command of 80th Motorised Brigade during the period from 20 to 24 November 1991. I take it you reviewed these findings. My question is: On the basis of the SFRY doctrine, which I understand to be the focus of your report, do you disagree or dispute any of these findings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I would appreciate if you would put -- I mean a concrete finding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: This question is far too general, Mr. Bourgon. There were lots of findings. I think that if you want to ask the witness a specific question, ask a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And I would counsel that you think of the time that you have. I'm anxious that you should be able to cover the areas that you really need.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was simply referring that whether there's any finding that he disputes. He saw the evidence. He can tell me if there's any findings that he disputes on the basis of doctrine. That's an important -- that's a very relevant question for this hearing. Are we relitigating or are we looking at a new fact. Is there any findings that he disputes? It's a very simple question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see how he handles it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor did not ask me to review the Trial Chamber judgement, so I haven't really looked into that. There may be things -- I mean, if you put a concrete thing in front of me I can maybe try to be of assistance, but it requires preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I still think if you have a specific question to ask about a finding made by the Trial Court about which you seek comment either in terms of accord or disagreement do ask it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will abide by your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, my -- I'd like to ask you a few questions now, coming back to what you said during your testimony before I move on. In your examination-in-chief you testified about -- at page 21, lines 15 to 22, about the difference between a commander -- not the difference. You said that as soon as Panic -- as soon as Mrksic left OG South Command, Panic became the acting commander; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But it's not an assumption, it's a fact because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm saying. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you used the word "assume."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, let me make that a bit clearer. Did you say that Panic was acting commander when Mrksic left the brigade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, and I do that on the basis of two documents. There's one order, the resubordination order --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with you. You don't need to explain.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just asking yes or no.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did Panic ever disagree in the evidence that he was standing in for Mrksic on that day?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That wasn't important to you if Panic accepted or did not accept that he was standing in?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't think that is what I'm saying. I don't remember Panic saying that he disagrees. That can mean two things: That my recollection is bad or that he indeed disagrees. I don't think he disagreed to that, and if he disagrees then there is a problem with the fact that he signed an order, a key order, at 6.00 in the morning on the 21st and he signs --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with you --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You don't need to explain. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quick questions. My next question: When Mrksic left Operational Group South command on the 21st in your opinion -- please yes or no, I don't want an explanation --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was he still the commander of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, there is no short answer to that question because obviously he goes as the commander of Operational Group South to Belgrade; however, because he's absent there is an acting commander who has all the duties and responsibilities of the commander of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony - because you spoke about this at page 21, lines 15 to 22. Now, let me give you a scenario and just tell me yes or no and we'll do the rest in writing, unless you feel obligated to explain of course. If Mrksic calls the brigade from Belgrade and he speaks to the operations officer, will the operations officer answer in your view: Sorry comrade Mrksic, I cannot speak to you today because you are away in Belgrade and my boss is Panic? Is that your view, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I can give you a very short answer. It depends what he calls for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But, I mean, if it's an operational matter why would -- if he calls the operations officer, it would mean that he cannot reach Panic, but then the operations officer would have the duty to ensure that Panic has all the information Mrksic -- operational information Mrksic shared with the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not the question again. Will the operations officer refuse to speak to him and to abide by instructions given to him by Mrksic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question because we have to first establish why would Mrksic call the operations officer for an operational matter when we know that actually his Chief of Staff is the acting commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again you're avoiding my question. I will move on to my next one. And I would like to now address your report and I would like to ask you some questions about your CV. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, sir, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, and what if the telephone call from Mrksic would say: I would suggest in light of my experience that this be done? How would you react to that? No order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was hoping that the expert would say. I'm saying that the commander is calling -- I was simply asking him. Will the operations officer say: I can't speak to you. You're away and I've got my commander here, or will he entertain the information? My position is he will entertain, but that's what the -- my question I asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not my answer, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps Mr. Theunens could be given a chance to answer that properly. I think he's being cut off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, you have been in the military. It wouldn't make sense for the operations officer to say to Mrksic: Sorry, I don't talk to you. I mean, it wouldn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that's all I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, but please. I mean, this is not one-liners. The operations officer will not keep Panic fully like -- how do you call it? Would not avoid to inform Panic about everything Mrksic tells him because his duty -- I mean, the operations officer, his duty is to ensure that he assists Panic in maintaining permanent situational awareness. So it may be that Mrksic calls Panic -- calls the operations officer, but then the operations officer, who has no command authority by the way, he will talk immediately to Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make that easier, sir. Mrksic calls --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and he speaks to Panic --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: To Panic, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he gives him an order. Will Panic refuse to execute the order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Normally not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move my next question. On the basis of my reading of your CV, I take it that you have no war experience, you've never been involved in a war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Sorry, if he would execute the order, how does this fit into your theory of unity of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, it could be -- but Mrksic is talking to Panic only. It could be that Mrksic, because he's in Belgrade, he receives an oral instruction, for example, from the command of the 1st Military District who is there. And then Mrksic is not going to order the commanders, like 80th Brigade or other subordinate units of OG South, no, he will speak to Panic because Panic is the commander on the ground. And then it will be Panic who issues orders on the basis again of the plans and another assistant -- assistance provided by his staff to the units, but Mrksic is not going to call in directly to the command of the 80th Brigade. It would go via Panic because Panic is the commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just to be clear about the situation. Assuming Mrksic would call directly the unit instead of going to Panic just because either he does not find the commander, Panic, on the phone, he -- or he has the number of the other one, whatever the reason, and gives the order -- an order to the head of the unit, is that your view that the unit commander will not implement the order without prior going to check to give the information to Panic and have Panic confirm the order? Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. Because Panic is the commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's very helpful. Now, let me move again to your CV.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I was just asking you that on the basis of your CV, please answer yes or no, you have never been involved yourself in a war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have held no command position in a war, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And no staff positions in the war either within a unit involved as a party to a conflict?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No -- I mean, the UN was not involved in a war, that's obvious. No, the Belgian armed forces were not involved in a war during the time I served in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your command experience, sir, is limited to when you -- at early on in your career when you were commander of a tank platoon which has four tanks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct. And I've been also acting a command of a company which has 13 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I tried to -- if I asked you to describe yourself in military terms, or if your colleagues would describe yourself in military terms, they would simply say that you are an intelligence officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm an intelligence analyst because an intelligence officer can be many things, it can be somebody who collects information and so on. Intelligence analyst would be a good definition, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate and I apologise because I fully agree with you. It's intelligence analyst I should have used. Now, you have never worked yourself in an operational brigade headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is not correct because -- I mean, two points. First, I've been a liaison officer between two brigades doing exercises with the Belgian armed forces, whereby I had a very close look at how a NATO brigade works, and I've also attended a one-year staff course in Belgium which was brigade level. And I've had -- during the time-period I worked here I saw many documents, I mean, regulations, operational reports, orders, as well as I had the privilege to interview a number of senior officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade, including Defence witnesses, so I think I'm in a position to issue a number of analytical conclusions in relation to how the Guards Brigade operated in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you work in an operational brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I was a liaison officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A liaison officer is not in a brigade --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you ever a G2?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But a liaison officer can work in a brigade because actually the liaison officer, he passes the information from one brigade commander to the other brigade commander. So I -- it's still a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you've never been a Chief of Staff, have you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to the methodology of your report, and I'd like to address what you said in answer to Judge Guney's question a little earlier, which is on page 31, lines 14 to 19: "What I have tried to do is to look at the testimony Mr. Panic has given and I compared it with SFRY armed forces doctrine or JNA military doctrine and I compared it with the other evidence that had been presented in the trial as well as the Trial Chamber's judgement and the Appeals Chamber judgement, and that is how I came to the conclusions." That's your statement that you said at page 31, lines 14 to 19 -- 13 to 14. I would just like to confirm that this is what you did in this case. That's what you tried to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This is actually how I implemented the methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean -- sorry, just to clarify, because maybe -- I mean, English is not my first English. I implemented the methodology, the intelligence side which I've also described in previous -- during previous testimony and I -- or I applied that methodology to the information that was in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on, talking about methodology and reference has been made to this by my colleague and by yourself. You use a number of documents, including trial Exhibit 578?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my report in the trial which was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's a comprehensive report of some 300 pages which addresses the concepts and the principles found in the doctrine that you talked about today?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this report was prepared for the Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin trial?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the footnotes in this report, I see, for example, the All People's Defence law, that was Exhibit 392; I see the manual for the work of commands and staff, that was 393; I see the JNA textbook on command and control, that was 394; I see the JNA brigade rules, that was 395; I see the regulations on the applications of the rules of international law, that was 396; and I look at JNA battalion manual, 397. Now, it's my understanding that your report for this review hearing is based on the same sources of doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, and you -- I think you listed a number of examples, yeah, the most relevant ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which ones did I miss?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't know by heart, but the other report I don't know how many exhibits I listed there. But I also looked -- and I think -- I mean some of the documents were presented by the Prosecution. I looked at also not just the doctrine but also how the Guards Motorised Brigade implemented the doctrine, i.e., I looked at orders and combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I know that. But --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- doctrine point of view, SFRY doctrine --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- is there anything that is in 578 that you look for this case that is not in 578, doctrine point of view?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would it be right to conclude then that those sources which form the basis of your report that was in evidence at trial, this was available to the Judges when they rendered their judgement in that case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I don't think I'm in a position to comment on how the Judges came to their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you would agree with me that you testified in this trial; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you explained the concepts developed in your report, 578?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed -- there's maybe one difference that I didn't really address the role of the Chief of Staff, and I think when you compare my report, Exhibit 578, with the report that is now in front of you, I tried to focus more on the duties according to SFRY armed forces doctrine of the Chief of Staff. So -- and that's why I think it's relevant to highlight these things because -- I mean, you know as well as I do, these regulations, some are 400 pages. You cannot expect somebody to look in at all these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's why you testified to explain it to the Judges at trial?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
