utterances.text: I don't decide myself about testimony. I was called, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to clarify because we -- I read your quote, you tried to explain it more. But looking at what you said today and in your report, what you really tried to do is you analysed the acts and conduct of Panic in light of the doctrine; that was your aim, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is what I was asked to do by the OTP appeals chamber [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to say whether it was in accordance with or consistent or not consistent with the doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: To a -- yeah. Or whether it was consistent not just with the doctrine but also to the -- again, the reports -- OG South regular combat reports as well as orders, i.e., how the doctrine was implemented. Because the doctrine as such is one thing, but you also have to compare it with how it is implemented, and if there are differences you try to understand these differences because there must be reasons. And what I noticed is that actually that the testimony of Mr. Panic -- and I don't want to talk too long, but I interviewed -- I had a lot to participate in the witness interview of Mr. Panic before he was a witness. And there was -- let's say there was -- the views were very coherent, doctrine and OG South how they implemented through the documents and the orders. I noticed that when I compared now his testimony in the pre-review hearing that there was significant differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to confirm that -- I want to confirm that when Panic was interviewed by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and he gave his statement for this trial -- for the trial --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- you were a member -- you were there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: And I think it's -- sorry, it's useful because at that time it wasn't clear whether he would be Prosecution or Defence or whatever. So -- or whether he would even be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my question now is when you say that you analysed the combat reports, which is the evidence, the doctrine, and the findings and then you say is it consistent or not with the doctrine, and if it's not consistent it's highly unusual or rather implausible, was that your methodology?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, that's not the methodology. Again, the methodology is the intelligence cycle more or less, and I would focus just on the processing phase; i.e., where you look at the information. First of all, you're going to verify the reliability of the source and the credibility of the -- first of all, you evaluate that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm talking what you did for this case --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, no, no, but that's the methodology, the intelligence cycle. And the processing phase where first I collate, I organise my information, okay, I receive a number of questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I look for -- I mean based on my recollection for documents, I look at relevant sections of the testimony. I looked at my previous report to see what -- which section was dealing with what. I noticed, for example, that there was not very much about the role of the Chief of Staff. So I thought okay, let's take again the regulations. I could establish that the regulations were a reliable source. Why? Because I participated in a number of interviews where these senior officers confirmed this was the regulation that we should apply. Then I start to -- in the analysis step of the processing phase, I compared the information, the new information, with the existing body of knowledge. That is what this analysis is about. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what you did in this case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you drew conclusions on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the new testimony in your view was against doctrine, you said it was highly unusual or rather implausible?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you always focus or you try to limit it just to doctrine. Doctrine is I would say -- I mean, the logic is I start with doctrine. And then I say like, how was the doctrine implemented by OG South, and I see that through the combat documents at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly. And then I compared it with my military experience which I have acquired at different moments -- even at this moment I still acquire military experience because UNIFIL is a quiet military mission. And when looking at all these three key elements I draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it you're familiar with the findings of the Trial Chamber with respect to the application of doctrine, how the doctrine was applied. I take it you're familiar with these findings? I'll bring them to your attention if you're not.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, that would be helpful just to avoid misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's begin, for example, the creation of OG South Command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber held at paragraph -- that was at paragraph -- sorry, paragraph 69 on page 24, they concluded that the creation of Operational Group South, okay, was established as an expedient to deal with a situation which had not been anticipated by the applicable formal rules, i.e., the internal breakup of the SFRY, and that Operational Group South did not strictly comply in structure to any formal formation. Do you agree with the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the fact that the normal -- another finding, I'll go straight to the point. Another finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 285, and I just want to know that you agree with this finding, and it's the following: "The Chamber is not able to accept that normal JNA procedures were consistently observed or regarding as so binding as Sljivancanin Defence has so strongly urged. The facts of this case disclosed frequent non-observance of normal JNA procedures and standards at all levels affecting matter as varied as the very establishment and structure of Operational Group South," okay, that's one, "but to the observance of the chain of command." Do you dispute that finding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's paragraph 285?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 285, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the sentence as it is in the transcript. Okay. When I read in the middle "and structure of Operational Group South, okay, that's one but to the observance of the chain of command."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me read it again. I'm sure the Judges, if I need, will at least entertain my request for more time if I need some. Let me read that quote. "The Chamber is not able to accept that normal JNA procedures were consistently observed or regarding as so binding." Do you agree with that? Do you dispute this finding?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You gave one example -- I mean the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, that's a finding. Do you dispute --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] You analysed the judgement --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, I didn't analyse the judgement, but I don't dispute what you just told me. I was not asked to analyse the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I know you weren't, but you did consider the judgement, that's what you said in your answer.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but not to analyse the judgement. The judgement was a source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you, yes or no, look at a number of trial judgement findings to do your report? They're all over the place in the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I mean it's maybe the matter of interpretation, but I did not analyse the judgement. I looked at the judgement and I -- for certain things -- where it was -- things were not clear to me, I used the judgement. Now, okay there are -- there may be doubt about the procedures as to how OG South was established. I think it was a complicated situation. But I haven't seen any -- I don't remember seeing, and again I worked very long on this trial also requesting documents I mean for years that there were -- that there was a pattern of a violation -- I mean the most basic principle of command and control, i.e., single authority. I haven't seen such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you disagree with the Trial Chamber's finding, and I will read you the quote, okay. "This case discloses" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, my colleague is standing up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, of course we have no problem with Mr. Bourgon putting this quote to the witness, but it has to be put in the context of the whole quote of the whole paragraph. This is in effect the prelude -- the Trial Chamber's prelude to its reasoning as to why it was not prepared to find beyond reasonable doubt and gave the benefit to Mr. Sljivancanin in his being involved in the transmission of the order. So I think that's a very important detail that Mr. Bourgon is not covering in his question and it's quite misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I disagree, Mr. President, but I will move on simply by reading the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the quote goes as follows, and that's part of the quote which can be isolated: "This case" -- okay, the facts of this case, we're not talking about a specific example here, "the facts of this case disclose frequent non-observance of normal JNA procedures and standards at all levels affecting matter as varied as the very establishment and structure of OG South to the observance of the chain of command." Do you agree or disagree with the Trial Chamber's finding?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have to give the same answer I gave earlier. It's a very general -- I mean kind of statement where, from an analytical point of view at least. If I were asked to analyse it and to give an opinion, well, then I would like to see examples. And on the basis of this example, so far I only heard one example, that was the establishment of OG South, and there I agree with you. But I don't think that that is a significant matter. And I tried to explain to you that the evidence I have reviewed and also -- I mean the documents -- the -- what I heard from various witnesses, violation of the principle of command and control, i.e., single authority, I haven't seen an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to my next question. I'd like to address a few issues in your report, and I will begin by question 1 which is found at page 3. Now, at the review hearing Panic testified - so you're familiar with that - that no commander is duty-bound to inform all of his subordinates of the orders that he issues. Panic also answered yes to the proposition put to him by Judge Meron that it is not impossible that Mrksic issued the withdrawal order directly to the 80th Motorised Brigade without telling his own Chief of Staff. Now, I personally fail to find a clear answer in your -- in question 1, but that's not what I want to discuss with you today --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I don't think it's correct what you say because I do say that -- I use the expression apos -- to inform Panic a posteriori in paragraph 8 where I do leave the door open that Mrksic would have spoken directly to Vojnovic. But then soon -- I mean, the order is implemented -- it is visible on the ground to what is the effect of the order, and then I would expect, well, if he doesn't do it in advance, which would have been logical because Mrksic needs input from his staff for that order. It's not just like move the truck 20 metres, it's a serious matter. And leaving the door open for the possibility that he could have issued the order directly to Vojnovic without telling anyone, as you suggest, even though he told Karanfilov as we know, then to me it would be highly unusual that he wouldn't inform Panic immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to my next question --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because the Judge covered that with you. In your report --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- does it say anywhere it's impossible that Mrksic did that either with prior or after notice, is it impossible? Do we find these words in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, because as I tried to explain we're working with human beings. Of course Mrksic can do it. But we have to look at the next step. Why do you issue an order? To have something done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: And the action would be visible. And so -- I mean, there would be an immediate effect and everybody would know. So of course Mrksic could tell Vojnovic, but where would it lead us to? Everybody would know immediately, i.e., contradicting what Panic has tried to explain during the pre-review hearing that nobody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a practical example and that will be much easier to cover this. Okay. Because the crux of the matter really, even if it was not addressed in direct examination, to us is at paragraph 14 of page 7, so if I can have that in e-court and that would be -- because you say in this report -- in this paragraph that the testimony of Panic that he was not aware of the order issued by Mrksic is inconsistent with SFRY armed forces doctrine. Okay. That's your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your report. Okay. So let's try -- what I would like to suggest to you is some reasons Mrksic might have had of doing so without informing Panic, and you can tell me if I'm out to left field or if what I'm saying makes a bit of sense. Let's try one possibility. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 621 that: "When Mrksic issued the withdrawal of the JNA Guards, he well knew that this left the TO and the paramilitary" units or -- sorry, units is not there, "with unrestrained access to the prisoners and that by enabling this he was assisting in the commission of the offences of violence and murder and that he was aware what indeed probably followed." Do you agree what really this means is that when Mrksic issued the withdrawal order he knew well that he was committing a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, that the absence of a person of Guards Motorised Brigade or OG South staff guarding the prisoners could or would result in crimes, yeah, could result in crimes. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it wasn't certain according to you or was it certain? It's very important. If the Trial Chamber says it is. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not referring to the trial judgement here. I'm just looking from the military point of view. Mrksic has received information actually throughout -- and actually the command of OG South, they all -- I mean they knew it, also the Chief of Staff. Panic himself is there on the 20th in the afternoon. He testified that he informed Mrksic. They know that something can happen, they have to foresee it, that's the duty -- I'm not referring to the judgement here. I'm just looking at military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, but that's very important that you would say this because you say that Panic knows and Mrksic knows. Now, very different -- very big difference here. Mrksic is withdrawing the MPs. He knows that there will be a crime. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: From the doctrinal point of view, on the basis that -- on the basis of the informations received, yeah, it could result in crimes, and he would be held accountable because he had a duty to foresee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the Trial Chamber said when he did this --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He knew very well.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with the Trial Chamber's judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you would agree with me then that when you look at SFRY doctrine, okay, at the way you referred it because I never found any term like that in the books, but --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Which term --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- if in all of these books [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Which term?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I never found the term "SFRY armed forces doctrine" in any of the sources you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, but doctrine is a concept. Doctrine is a set of regulations for which -- I mean for military doctrine military behaviour is based. The SFRY armed forces should be a known entity. I mean, they were established -- I don't have the exact reference here, but I think it's referred in my document when the name changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But to put that all together this concept --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and you say number of books is your call; right? You decide what is SFRY armed forces doctrine. That's what you told the Judges when you testified?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't decide that. That is what I think what also senior officers of the JNA have told us, that, okay, the doctrine said this and they referred to the same kind of regulations I did. So I didn't invent something knew here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In that doctrine, in that doctrine --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- is there anything that says that when a commander is going to commit a crime he has to inform his Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, I don't understand -- again, I come back to the point, the order -- no, no, you cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's simple, it's simple --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there anything in the book -- is there a rule that says that if I'm about to commit a crime I have to tell my Chief of Staff if I'm the commander. It's a very simple question. Yes or no? Find me the rule.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this question is nonsensical from the military point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to my next question --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But I would like to mention. You cannot look at an order. An order is not something in isolation. Why do you give an order? Not just to issue a document. No. You issue an order to have an action executed. That action here consists of withdrawing the MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Ovcara was, I don't know, less than 10 kilometres away from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, we agree that the order is a crime?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It would result in a crime, yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you're not sure whether it could or not result in a crime? It's very important. From a military point of view, because you say it's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no. Your question is nonsensical. I didn't say that the order is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, but is the order -- do you agree, yes or no, that Mrksic knew that he was committing a crime? That's what the Trial Chamber said.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I go along with the Trial Chamber's judgement. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then my question is: Find me a rule where it says the commander has to tell his Chief of Staff if he's committing a crime, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I cannot answer your question in the context of like when I look at SFRY armed forces documents, the facts, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on because I think the Trial Chamber will. But let's look at another example -- sorry, the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we look at the facts of this case as established by the Trial Chamber. Now, you will agree with me based on the facts that Mrksic did not issue the withdrawal order or mention the withdrawal order during the daily briefing, did he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, that is -- I think what is stated in the judgement and the evidence. I don't know -- why how -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, but your conclusion did he say it in the daily briefing yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I haven't looked into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be important to know whether it was mentioned because one of your conclusions is that Panic should have mentioned it at the daily briefing. Did you not look to see if the commander mentioned it at the daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no. What I wrote is that -- I mean, Panic testified that he informed the commander Mrksic about what he had seen in Ovcara and he'd also asked Mrksic to take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are at one step further.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are at the withdrawal order, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed. But when I write that Panic should have mentioned it during the briefing, I would expect that Panic would also -- because the briefing everybody is together there, the people from Ovcara are there Vojnovic, that Panic would check with them in -- of course in close co-ordination with Mrksic, like how is the situation now? Because we are three or four hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you have expected the commander to mention this order at the daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: If the order had been taken already then it should have been mentioned, but I don't remember exactly when the order was given. I think it's only later that the people are informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- do you agree, reveals that it was not mentioned at the daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All right. So let's put that aside. You agree, then, that Panic did not learn this order at the daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We're together on this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, let's go a bit further and you say that -- and of course, and the fact that Mrksic did not mention this is also a violation of the doctrine because a commander should share with his staff; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It depends when he decides to issue that order. If he decides to issue it after the meeting, then obviously he cannot mention it during the meeting. If he had decided to issue the order and if he issued it prior to the meeting, he should have mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. He should have mentioned it, and if he did not it's a violation of the doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, it depends on the timing of the order. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So all this is a grey area?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, it's not a grey area. I don't have the trial judgement in front of me but I don't remember exactly when Mrksic issued the order to withdraw the MPs. I'm just trying to clarify my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Well I will help you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber held that the order was issued shortly before or shortly after the daily briefing. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, if it's before the daily briefing he should have told them. If it's after the daily briefing, then he should have communicated it otherwise. But he cannot -- if it's issued after the briefing he cannot mention it during the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but can you give us the reference to the judgement that you've made just then on the finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Earlier or after?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. That one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll find it and get back to you unless you want it now because I'm quite short of time, but of course that's a finding that we have in the judgement and I forgot to have it here in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But let me look then -- we know from the evidence, and you referred to that, that Mrksic then met with Vojnovic, and he gave his order only to Vojnovic at that time? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think there's also Vukosavljevic in the area. I know of that. But again let's be careful not to think in exclusives. The fact that we can establish to whom he gave it does not exclude that he would have given it to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this is criminal law --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have a judgement, we have findings, and I'm willing to entertain any dispute or challenges on your part because I think that that's what your whole report is about, relitigating this case.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bourgon, Colonel Panic, if I remember correctly, himself testified on a number of occasions - and this is in the exhibits which have been submitted to us - that he would be tremendously surprised that it would be completely exceptional for Mrksic not to share the order with him at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's one of my questions coming up, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Also, the testimonies of Mr. Panic suggest and they were given before the trial judgement, I quite agree, suggest that on the whole OG South functioned well in terms of transmission of orders. There may have been -- he mentions one or two sort of exceptions, but on the whole he's much more flattering to the performance of OG South than the Trial Chamber was in the sentence that you have cited. It's a complex issue and it's really quite difficult to -- but I would really suggest that since your time is limited, try to focus as much on the problems that you are trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let us look at the facts of the case that Mrksic, we agree -- you know from the evidence that he did not say it at the daily briefing. But you mentioned in your testimony that he said it to two people.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He said it to Karanfilov and he said it to Vojnovic, probably in the presence, we're not sure, of Vukosavljevic. That's the evidence. Okay. Now, what I'm simply suggesting to you: If a commander, okay, is about to issue an illegal order and -- no, not about, has issued an illegal order to two subordinates, would that be a fair thing to say, that he's not going to -- he will limit this to as few individuals as possible simply to protect himself. Is that a possibility, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It doesn't -- if -- I mean, the order is intended to carry out an activity. Now, the activity consists of withdrawing forces. Everybody will see that the forces are gone and they will ask what happened. And the only logical conclusion is that the commander, because there is single authority, has issued the order to withdraw them. So he cannot hide that. Karanfilov, it would be highly unlikely that Mrksic, again according to doctrine and what we've seen in the trial, that Mrksic would talk directly to Karanfilov ignoring Vukasinovic, i.e., the deputy of the security organs and most importantly ignoring Sljivancanin who was actually in charge of this operation where then Mrksic, according to you, would just talk to a captain to say, look, let's get them out of there. It wouldn't make sense because within minutes everybody would know, and Sljivancanin would hear it from Karanfilov, and he would go to Mrksic and say, colonel, what are you doing. That would be the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me just get one question on this because if I listen to you correctly I take it that 20 military policemen who are in Ovcara, they return to their barracks or wherever they live, okay, at the command or in or around the command of the 80th Brigade. That's your position that within minutes everybody will know that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, because -- I mean, I'm not talking about the 20 military policemen, I'm talking about Karanfilov. If Mrksic talks to Karanfilov directly, I mean Karanfilov should be -- should ask himself, should check with Sljivancanin, hey, the commander has told me that, it's your operation, how do you see that. I mean that would be the logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, that's not what you said. You said within minutes people will know that the MPs have been withdrawn and they will say commander what did you do? Are you saying that --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, I -

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 20 men leaving from Ovcara and returning to OG South -- not OG South, returning to the 80th Brigade. I just want to know if it's your professional opinion that within minutes everyone will know in OG South. Is that your professional opinion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I will give you two elements of reply. First of all, it's not about the 20 men. It's about handing over authority from OG South to another entity. That is a key issue. Secondly, I mean you are familiar with the inspection function of command and control and also the fact that they have to report on the implementation of the order. So in concrete terms the MPs will inform the operations centre of the 80th Brigade, hi, we're back, and the operations centre of the 80th Brigade will inform the operations centre of the OG South, gentlemen, we have implemented your mission, they are now back in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now if I look at what you're saying now, okay, is there any evidence on the record that there was a report made to Operational Group South Command, did you see any evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, there is no such evidence, but again if Karanfilov -- I think it's established -- it is established in the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, is there a finding --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Karanfilov -- it is established Karanfilov goes to Ovcara to tell the MPs of the 80th Brigade to withdraw. Karanfilov has to come back to the OG South and say: I have passed the order. They are withdrawing. That is military reality, and I don't know whether the Trial Chamber confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So -- well, the Trial Chamber did not.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So but I'll ask you if I want to confirm that today, I need to call Karanfilov to testify again; right? That's what you want if you want to determine that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no. I mean there is a finding that Karanfilov knew about the order because he informed the 80th Brigade, and then again based on how militaries work, Karanfilov reports to his commander to his -- actually, he should report to Sljivancanin, I have implemented your order, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But is there evidence to that that you saw. You looked at the evidence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I didn't look at all the evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that was not interesting to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That's not the issue. I don't think it -- I mean, it's probably not -- it's not mentioned in the -- I don't know whether it's mentioned in the trial judgement or the Appeals Chamber's judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned that three people were made aware of that order: Karanfilov, Vukosavljevic, and Vojnovic. You will agree with me we can add to this, we can add a Vezmarovic because he's the guy who withdrew the MPs. So that's four people; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean you can add the 20 MPs if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the 20 MPs. Yes. Okay. Now, let me tell you is there any finding in the judgement of anybody else who was informed of that order, is there any findings in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have not analysed the judgement. That was not the tasking I have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thought you were going to compare the judgement with the findings and the SFRY doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not what you did?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, I compared the testimony of Mr. Panic with the doctrine with the operational -- I mean, the combat documents, i.e., reports and orders of OG South. And indeed I received a copy of the trial judgement and the appeals judgement. But I haven't looked in -- I haven't -- those were sources. But it was not my duty or my -- I was not requested to analyse these sources in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to a quick question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I really don't think that it was within his remit to come with a notation on the judgement as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, Mr. President, but it was his job to look at the judgement. He said he did. How can he make a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I mean, he was given a specific remit by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll save that for argument, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think he was given a specific remit by the Prosecution and he tried to carry that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is it a possibility, possibility, that Mrksic -- and there's a reference to this in the judgement at the finding in paragraph 586, okay, where it says that there are suspicions to that effect. Is it possible that Mrksic received an order from superior command and the order is: Give them the prisoners, we cannot avoid a conflict with these people at this time? Is that a possibility, sir, that in such a case, okay, if the order said: Don't tell anyone, that Mrksic would not tell anyone? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, I have tried to explain that "don't tell anyone" doesn't work in the military because the people have left. OG South will familiarise themself -- I mean Panic when he's the commander, he has to be really sure that what he tells to the 1st military district is correct. He will have a look at what is happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You cannot hide that there are no more MPs in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When a crime is committed --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. It's not what you say that there is no don't tell. I'm just asking you, okay, and we'll go to another scenario and that will be my last one.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You -- Panic said when he testified, first of all, he said that Panic -- sorry, that Mrksic should have told him. So you and him agree on this. No problem there. Then Panic said: If I had heard this during the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin, if I had heard this, I would immediately have reacted. Okay. Now, you agree with me that this would have been the thing to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, given that this was the thing to do, I'm simply suggesting to you the possibility, okay, that Mrksic, he knew very well that Panic would oppose this order and that's why he did not tell him. Is that a possibility, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But -- I'm sorry, I'm repeating myself, but it doesn't work like that. I mean, Panic is the Chief of Staff. He will be informed of the fact that the MPs are not there anymore, especially since on the 20th Panic goes out of his own initiative to Ovcara to see what is happening. Why could -- I mean, I cannot imagine that Mrksic would think like I can hide the order and Panic will certainly not have a look on the 21st, he will not be interested anymore. It doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if there are no findings that Panic found this information, what you're saying is that he's a liar; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I don't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you met with him. Did he look to you as a reasonable person?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will reserve my comments for myself. I've never commented on a witness and I will never do so, I mean not in this environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But did he co-operate with you when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Overall yes, but we had to use at certain occasions documents to clarify certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now to go on and move on. It is curious, Mr. Bourgon, that having visited Ovcara and brought back a rather worrying situation about dangers to which the POWs were exposed and the treatment which was being meted out to them, that Panic on the following day did not show any interest regarding the sequence, what happened later. This is a bit puzzling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will then go straight to a line of questioning referring to what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Liu has a question. Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you a question. I would like to draw your attention to your report on the paragraph 10 on page 6. You said that: "Considering the SFRY armed forces doctrine and the operational context, any suggestion that Mrksic would have tried to hide his withdrawal order from his closest collaborator and the deputy Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic and the officer he had put in charge of the evacuation operation Sljivancanin, appeared to be rather implausible." Did you find that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I would like you to explain to me how could I arrive in this conclusion and what SFRY armed forces doctrine you mean and what that operational context in your mind when you're writing this report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I will try to be brief. The reference to SFRY armed forces doctrine refers to the aspect of a situational awareness, whereby the staff managed or organised by the Chief of Staff is responsible for ensuring the situational awareness of the commander. And that is something I have addressed in question 1 where you can find the different regulations. So of course the commander has the legal duty to be aware, but he is assisted by his staff and there the Chief of Staff is the organiser. The operational context, just two elements. Ovcara I think is I wrote here less than 10 kilometres, but in fact is shorter, from Negoslavci. There was no -- I'm not aware of any impediment for members of the OG South Command to visit Ovcara at any moment in time on the 20th or the 21st. So -- and that's what I've tried to explain to Mr. Bourgon. The order as such doesn't mean anything. It is the effect of the order. I.e., when it is implemented it will have a result on the situation, and in this particular case on the situation of the friendly force, i.e., the units of OG South, where a number of forces have been withdrawn, more importantly prisoners of war which were under the control of OG South are now -- have been handed over to another entity and all that is part of the situational awareness where the Chief of Staff has the duty to inform the commander of these events and of these developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is there any evidence on the record that you saw of anyone noticing the departure of these 20 MPs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will give two --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, the evidence on the record, please. Do you see any?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I think the war diary or the operational diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade has an entry for the 20th in the evening that the military police of the 80th Brigade has returned to the -- yeah, the 80th Brigade, and that the prisoners have been handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see any evidence of this information reaching Operational Group South Command at any time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, actually the issue should not be -- should not be evidence of it reaching because that is common sense in the military. The evidence should have been -- or the question should have been not reaching. Because if that information -- if the 80th Brigade has not informed OG South then OG South has to tell the 80th Brigade what is happening, why didn't you tell us? Because we issued you an order we have to be informed of the implementation, that's how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely agree, as long as they know what the order is; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If they don't know the order they can't expect a come-back; right? Can they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I am told that you, when you speak you speak too quickly for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. No, because the order -- as I -- the order is one thing, but it's the effect of the order, implementation, that is the key issue, and the implementation is very visible. I have also tried to explain in my report that situational awareness is not a passive duty. You don't sit and wait like, is somebody going to tell me they have withdrawn. No. The commander has the duty to inform himself about the situation of his troops. Because you can -- I mean, it's like everywhere. Nobody is going to tell bad news or like to give bad news. So the commander has to be active, send these guys, invite the commanders of subordinate units like to know what is happening, and that is all part of the picture that is being created with the assistance of the staff under the management of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position then that if the doctrine says a report should have been sent back, then unless we have evidence that it was not we are to believe it was. That's your position?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No. My position is that if the report was not sent then OG South should have complained to the 80th Brigade what is happening, why don't you send the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If they don't know that the order was given they can't; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But it's their duty to know what is happening --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If the order was not given, can they expect a back order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: But if the order was not given they couldn't withdraw, because then that's anarchy. Militaries act upon orders and orders have to be -- everything has to be verified. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, my colleague reminded you that we have to focus on the findings of the Trial Chamber, okay, and we're not here to relitigate.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber found that there's no report going back to Operational Group South command. Okay. Vojnovic testified that he never told Mrksic that he had executed the order and that he had never told anyone for that matter. None of the persons that you say were aware of this order were found to have shared it with somebody with Panic. Nobody -- you mentioned those who are aware. Okay. You said the MPs. You said Vezmarovic. You said Vukosavljevic, you said Vojnovic, okay, and I'm going to add another one -- and of course Karanfilov, and I'm going to add another one to this and that's P14.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. And P14, okay, he discussed and they knew about the fate of the prisoners or they had rumours about the fate of the prisoners on the morning of 21st; whereas, the information in OG South according to the evidence was nil, and the information according to the record did not reach Operational Group South. Are they supposed to expect a back order when they are not even aware that the order was implemented?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on because I'll keep this for argument. One more issue I'd like to address with you. Now, Vojnovic when he received this order, now this man accepted to carry out an illegal order, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: With hindsight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mean he did not know on the spot?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, you would have to ask Vojnovic. Vojnovic -- one could -- one could argue that Vojnovic should have known that the withdrawal of the MPs could have resulted in crimes, yeah, that's Article I think 36 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So he accepted to carry out an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We have a question from Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in light of the irregularity of the order itself, would it not be expected to have it transmitted irregularly as well? This is the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: The second question is: Are you aware of another illegal order that was transmitted through the regular chain of command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To answer the first part, I think -- I mean, that's only a partial aspect because of course we can imagine the situation that Mrksic tries to hide the order -- I mean, let's develop a scenario. We could try to imagine that scenario, that he hides the issuing of the order. But it's about the effect of the order, the implementation, because the order as such as long as it is not implemented has no value. It's the implementation of the order which is a key issue here. And -- okay, Mr. Bourgon disputes that it would be noticeable to the command of OG South when I say in a very short time-period. On the 21st of November, OG South reports that everything is going in according with the regulations, i.e., the evacuation of the civilians and the wounded and the Geneva Conventions, whereas it was their duty to verify the situation, the status of the prisoners at Ovcara. Coming back to the second part of your question, I'm not aware of any other example of an -- call it illegal order that was transmitted via the regular or irregular manner. I'm not aware of such an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, how much time do I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Three minutes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I can be an accountant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I will -- I have two questions, then, that I will ask you, and the first one is the following. You know because you saw the appeal judgement's findings that we are here to discuss a new fact which was accepted by the Trial Chamber as being a new fact, which is that Panic heard a conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin and that during that conversation Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the military police. Now, that's why we are here today. Okay. I would like to know from you since you were involved or invited by the Prosecution to take part in these proceedings, were you -- was any additional evidence not known to the Trial Chamber at the time brought to your attention concerning this conversation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The -- I mean, the material I used -- or the material I used -- I received -- I apologise, from the OTP appeals section is identified in the introduction. I looked at military regulations, but I haven't seen any additional material -- or any additional evidence in relation to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, the Prosecution I take it did not discuss any such evidence with you, say, listen, we've got something here that we did not know of? That never came up; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, no, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you've been an analyst with the Office of the Prosecutor in the Military Analysis Team for quite a while or you were for a number of years, so you're quite familiar with these cases. And I take it that you are familiar with the fact that within the JNA officers and all members of the JNA are quite scared or at least do not like security officers, members of the security branch, because they can file a report at any time against anybody? Are you familiar in general with this concept?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it -- it's a bit of a -- maybe -- if you allow me, a liberal interpretation of doctrine, but there was some -- it's like in any armed force, I guess, some kind of, I mean, fear of security organs because they only show up at the bad moment. But it's not in writing, this is just interpretation of the people. It's never a good thing when a security officer comes to you because he may have something against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he may -- and security officers because of this special chain they have, they can make an investigation against a commander without a commander even knowing about it. You're familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, indeed, I mean more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if Mrksic has committed a crime by withdrawing the MPs, okay, I suggest to you that the last person he would tell this to is the security officer who can make an investigation on him; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, I don't because Article 36, as I mentioned, from the 1988 regulations on the implementation of the laws of war says that any officer whenever he discovers that a crime may have been committed has a duty to report it and, sorry, to provide information to the competent authorities. So the particular position of the security organs does not apply to these kind of crimes, I mean crimes -- a violation of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We really have to end this now, and of course, Mr. Bourgon, Karanfilov belonged to the security organ, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, why don't you just merge it with your summary later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will do so, Mr. President, because if he's scared of telling Sljivancanin, of course he would not tell Sljivancanin either that he told Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now have a 20-minute pause which is required by technical reasons. Ms. Brady, I am aware that you have both 15 minutes which have been allotted to you and subsequently the 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we will keep your rights to those two sections. 20 minutes, so we will meet at about 25 minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I, as I said before we recessed briefly, you have 15 minutes for the examination of the witness and then 30 minutes for your summary argument. And if you do not really need the entirety of these 45 minutes, we will not regret it if you cut it short.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have only two questions in re-examination, so that will definitely be quite short. Perhaps I could borrow from that time for a little bit of extra time for my submissions if need be, but we'll get to that at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I want to ask you, firstly, it relates to the question that you were asked right at the end by Mr. Bourgon about the order having gone to Mr. Karanfilov, Mrksic's order having gone to Karanfilov. And just to ask you, in the normal chain of events how would such an order to a subordinate in a security organ, how would it travel up to the head of that security organ?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The normal -- I'm sorry. The normal procedure would have been that Colonel Mrksic would have spoken to Major Sljivancanin and informed him directly, in particular because for this specific operation Sljivancanin was also in charge of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: But if we take the scenario that somehow -- that Mrksic gave the order directly to Karanfilov --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- how under normal military procedures would that information have travelled to his boss, the head of the security organ, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Karanfilov at the earliest possible time would inform Sljivancanin, and even prior to that he could ask Mrksic: Have you spoken to my commander -- I mean to my chief, i.e., Sljivancanin. And then Mrksic could explain to Karanfilov why he was not following the regular chain of command. But Sljivancanin would have to be informed as soon as possible by Karanfilov because otherwise it would be a violation of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the only other question I have for you in re-examination is Mr. Bourgon pointed out - this is at transcript page 70 of today's proceedings - that the OG South couldn't be expected to inquire about the implementation of the withdrawal order if it was not generally known that it had been issued. Now, what I'm interested in hearing is your view, even if Panic didn't know of the withdrawal order, does that mean -- doesn't that mean he had a duty to inform himself about the previous 24 hours activities of the 80th Motorised Brigade when he was acting commander on the 21st? So maybe if I could repeat. Even if Panic didn't know of that withdrawal order, didn't he have a duty to inform himself in any event about what had been going on 24 hours before vis-a-vis the 80th and vis-a-vis the prisoners, assuming - if we go to Panic's mind - that they're still there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, as I've tried to explain during cross-examination, the order is one thing and the implementation is another thing and is actually the most important aspect. In accordance with the need to ensure situational awareness not only at the level of the OG South but also at the level of OG South superior command, i.e., the 1st Military District, OG South was obliged to provide accurate and complete reporting on its activities. We have explained how they obtained that information. And so in order to provide that accurate and complete report on their activities, they would inquire on the situation Ovcara, as it is located in the zone of responsibility of OG South. And sooner or later somebody, I mean, would have discovered that the MPs are not there anymore. Again, that's in the scenario that nobody was informed about the order. The effect of the order, it cannot be hidden and that is what I've tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for Mr. Theunens, so I think he can be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the Appeals Chamber thanks you very much for having come today and having provided your written report and having testified today, and in the name of my colleagues and I'm sure also of the parties, I would like to thank you. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If my colleagues have questions to the Prosecution, perhaps it would be wise to do that after her summary arguments, but if somebody has a question now that the Judge feels should be asked now you are of course free to -- there are no questions now. So, Ms. Brady, your summary argument. You have 30 minutes, but I am aware of the fact that you have not used up your time for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honours, Panic's evidence that he didn't hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin on the evening of the 20th of November about his order to withdraw the JNA from Ovcara has no impact on the verdict because he cannot be believed on this matter. And we say this for three main reasons. First, self-interest. His evidence about the conversation is unreliable because what -- because of what it might suggest about his own knowledge of Mrksic's patently illegal order and his own responsibility for its disastrous consequences, and this follows the same pattern of evidence that he gave at trial. Second, bias. His evidence is unreliable because -- in addition, I should say, because of his demonstrated bias for the Guards Brigade and Sljivancanin. In our submission he's tailored parts of his testimony both at trial and in this review so as to best insulate himself and Sljivancanin from any knowledge of the order and thereby any responsibility for the crime. Third, implausibility. It is inconceivable given JNA military doctrine and the context of these events that Panic, the Chief of Staff who was acting commander the next day, remained ignorant of the withdrawal order throughout the evening of the 20th of November and then for the entire four days that he and the Guards Brigade stayed in Vukovar. These lies render his testimony about what he heard Mrksic say to Sljivancanin, or rather, not say to Sljivancanin simply not credible. Mr. Theunens' report and his evidence that we've just heard help to illuminate the lies and the half-truths that Panic had to tell this Chamber in order to support his claim of ignorance. And when seen in light of normal military doctrine, it's clear that Panic acted we could say most unusually from the time the withdrawal order was issued. And when this becomes apparent, one begins to see why the Trial Chamber treated his evidence so cautiously. Panic is obviously a highly professional -- successful, professional soldier. He's highly decorated. When he contravenes the military rules he's always lived by, you have to ask yourself why. When he buries his head in the sand, you have to ask yourself why. And when he lies to you, you have to ask yourself why. And this afternoon what I'm going to do with the rest of the session here is to highlight some of the most glaring occasions when Panic, on his own account, acted unusually. In the context of his broader knowledge, there's only one conclusion as to his motive for doing so. And of course we will be relying on our written submissions to make our argument in more detail. I'll turn first to his self-interest. The Trial Chamber observed Panic testify for four days and assessed his credibility at length, and these findings were upheld by this Chamber. It concluded that it could not believe his evidence when it came to matters that could expose him to criminal liability or which could put him in an unfavourable light. And, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber had this to say about Mr. Panic, and I'm quoting from 297 of -- paragraph 297 of the trial judgement. "Regrettably the Chamber also finds that in his evidence Lieutenant-Colonel Panic sought to present aspects of his own role in a more favourable light and to avoid disclosing matters that could be construed as implicating Panic himself in criminal conduct. Because of this, while the Chamber is entirely persuaded it should accept much of his evidence, it has and will identify its reservations about some issues." Now, what I'd like to do is just to take you briefly to three examples from trial where the Trial Chamber had these reservations and did not believe Panic. And you'll see that Panic's knowledge of the withdrawal order or lack of knowledge, as he claims, is of the same nature of evidence and for the same reason you should disbelieve it. First, the question of what Panic saw at the barracks, the JNA barracks, in the morning before he phoned Mrksic prior to going to the SAO government meeting. The Trial Chamber found that Panic "underplays the full extent of his knowledge of the situation at the barracks that morning" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could we have the paragraph in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. I'm quoting from paragraph 297 of the trial judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Still from the same paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It is. It's a different part. It's a very long paragraph. That he "underplays the full extent of his knowledge of the situation at the barracks that morning" and was "not fully frank and honest about the events he saw at the barracks concerning the convoy of prisoners of war." You will recall that here was a situation where Panic said there was one bus, no real security threat. The Trial Chamber found there were actually five buses there at that time and already the TOs were verbally and physically assaulting the prisoners on the bus. That's an example of minimising what he saw. Second, why Panic visited Ovcara after the government meeting. The Trial Chamber found his reason for going to Ovcara, remember he said he was going there to check on the progress of the trials, they found it "entirely lacking in credibility" and found instead that he went there in fact to assess the situation so he could make a report to Mrksic. That's at paragraph 307. Another example where he is minimising or downplaying his role or knowledge. Finally, what Panic saw at Ovcara. Again, the Trial Chamber found that he was "not being frank when speaking of his own knowledge of mistreatment of the prisoners of war that day, so as to minimise the truth in that respect." That's at paragraph 308. So while they did accept that he went and told Mrksic, you know, there's a security situation, you better -- you should send some further -- some further forces to deal with it, they accepted him on that but they found that he was not willing to admit the full extent of what he said because he was basically saying it was under control at that point, again to minimise himself from information that could really harm him. Panic's denial of any knowledge of the withdrawal order in this review proceeding follows that same pattern, as we can see from his trial evidence. Panic has repeatedly denied any knowledge of who ordered the withdrawal of the JNA security from Ovcara. So it's no surprise that he's come in these proceedings and continued to say or said he didn't hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal order that evening. It's a consistency. He's always said he didn't know, so of course from his point of view he's going to say he didn't hear. Because to admit hearing this - and, Your Honours, allowing the Appeals Chamber's finding to stand would have the same effect because he's privy to that conversation in accordance with the finding that you made - if he admits hearing that conversation he too would have been privy to that illegal order, something that he has never admitted to, can never admit to, because it would mean that he did nothing to stop it. So in our submission his self-interest in the events gives him every reason to hide the truth on what was said that evening at the command post between Mrksic and Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do mind refreshing my memory, Ms. Brady, did we make a specific finding regarding Panic listening to the order that was given, according to us, by Mrksic to Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I believe that Panic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You say that he was privy and that we so found. Would you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Did we --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Paragraph 62 of the appeals judgement in a footnote -- excuse me, Your Honours, I thought that it had been footnoted in that part of the judgement, but nevertheless that was the evidence at trial of Sljivancanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But that was your conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- and Panic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But when you said that we so found, this is not quite so, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you made the finding that when Sljivancanin went in to report to Mrksic, the conversation had occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I simply did not remember our alluding in that context to the presence of Panic, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to double-check that because you've quoted -- I think this is the reasoning, actually. You've quoted from Veselin Sljivancanin's testimony, the trial testimony. And in that there's reference to the fact that Panic was there at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. If you have something to add you can always --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- insert a short sentence in your summary. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I will carry on. The second point bias. Panic's self-interest has to be considered together with the clear bias that he exhibits for the Guards Brigade and Sljivancanin. Panic spent almost a quarter of his career with the Guards Brigade and his reputation is clearly bound up with theirs. He was Chief of Staff at the time. The next year he was made commander. We will be detailing this more in our brief. But he well knows that the impact of the Ovcara massacre on the reputation of the Guards Brigade -- and, Your Honours, I would like to remind you how Panic -- Mr. Panic opened his testimony in the Belgrade trial in the 2004 Belgrade trial, this is Exhibit Number 1, and I'm quoting from page 15. He said this, this is how he opened: "Allow me to say, first of all, that I'm very sorry and upset that it has come to this. That team of officers of the Guards Brigade or the Guards Brigade itself did not deserve this. What happened happened, a job done professionally, and here in the end the Guards Brigade is being called to account, so what can I say about that?" The image that Panic wants to project here in this proceeding is that of a neutral observer only wanting the truth. That image is some way from reality. And again we will be going through this more in our written submissions. This is just a summary form of that argument. But what is more interesting is that you can actually see Panic's bias in his trial evidence. You will recall at trial the rather major shift in Panic's testimony when for the first time at trial he named Pavkovic as having been the person in charge of the evacuation, and he said, "Well, Sljivancanin was only in charge of the security tasks at the hospital." And the Trial Chamber noted that that diverged sharply from his 2000 -- his previous statement that he'd given in 2005, that's Exhibit 2 in these proceedings, because in that statement Panic had said that he was present at the command briefing the night before when Mrksic placed Sljivancanin in charge of the evacuation and could use as many military police as possible. So at trial he did an about-face and the Trial Chamber relied on his statement and what was the contents of his statement rather than that trial testimony. This is a finding that the Appeals Chamber upheld on appeal. Another example of his bias can be seen in his claim that it appeared from the government meeting that they planned to try the prisoners of war, something he told Mrksic. And the Trial Chamber said at paragraph 585 that it was "quite unable to accept the honesty of this aspect of his evidence. It was obviously self-serving and ... an attempt to put the JNA and Mile Mrksic in a more favourable light." And, Your Honours, in our submission his bias is also evident in these current -- in this present review proceeding. When he testified in the review hearing he mentioned two additional topics of discussion in that conversation which had not appeared previously in his statement which he gave to Mr. Lukic last year in 2009. This is Exhibit 4. Where he was writing down his recollection of that conversation. When he came here at the review he gave two other bits of information, we call it, that hadn't appeared in the statement about that discussion, one, that Sljivancanin had reported to Mrksic that he was back from his mission; and two, that the government had decided to take the prisoners to Ovcara. And it's no coincidence in our submission that these matters had featured as part of Sljivancanin's trial testimony and then they appear now in the review hearing. We'll -- again, we'll be detailing these inconsistencies in our brief in more beet. In summary on these two points, Panic's account of the conversation should be given no weight given his powerful incentive to protect himself, his revered unit, and Sljivancanin. Before I turn to my third point which is the other reason you shouldn't believe him, I wanted to clarify that in answer to your question you did actually make the finding that in paragraph 61 of the trial -- of the appeals judgement that, it's about five lines from the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I was thinking it was a footnote to paragraph 62, but in fact it's in paragraph 61, Your Honours. You recall basically what Sljivancanin did when he got back to the command post, and in the middle of it you have said: "Sljivancanin then met with Captain Borisavljevic who told him about the meeting of the SAO government" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's in paragraph 61?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: And then it says, and this is the relevant part for us: "Finally Sljivancanin met with Mrksic and Panic." That's the reference I'm talking about when I say Panic knows that he's named as part of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: There is no direct mention here of the withdrawal order in that context in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but if you put paragraphs 61 and 62 here, what you've said is that Sljivancanin went to see Panic -- went and had a conversation with Mrksic and Panic, and the next -- very next paragraph you've said that in the course of that meeting Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin of the order. So I think the logical implication, at least to an outside reader, is that Panic was there and that's something that Panic himself could well recognise if somebody picked up that judgement and read it about themselves they would say, "Well, you know, I'm also part of that discussion about an illegal order." I'll move now to my third reason as to why you shouldn't believe Panic, and that is that his evidence is implausible in light of JNA military doctrine.
