Now, this Chamber has not had the same opportunity as the Trial Chamber did to observe Panic testifying for four days, but even from the comparatively brief evidence that he gave in June of this year, in the pre-review hearing, it's clear that he's not telling the truth. Now, we have to remember a few things. First, on the 20th of November Panic was the Chief of Staff and he'd already played a significant role regarding the prisoners that day, being the conveyor of Mrksic's order to the government meeting, and he knew about the precariousness of their situation. The next day, the 21st of November, he took over from Mrksic as acting commander. His testimony that he wasn't aware of the withdrawal order during this whole period, from the evening of the 20th of November and then throughout the remaining four days that he and the Guards stayed in Vukovar, simply defies military doctrine. Because to believe Panic would mean that three core principles of military doctrine - and I'm talking about singleness of authority and unity of command and situational awareness, the duty to be situationally aware - that these core principles had completely broken down in this highly disciplined and elite unit of the JNA. Now, firstly Panic's evidence when he says he didn't know of the withdrawal order that evening, this defies military doctrine. And we say this, first, because he was the Chief of Staff and we've heard today and in the report that under the JNA armed forces military doctrine, that person, the Chief of Staff, plays a central role in the commander's work. He's the principal advisor to the commander, he's the deputy, he's got to be there waiting -- able, I should say, to take over if something bad happens to the commander. He works closely with him to formulate orders and decisions and implement them. It's almost -- these are my words, not the expert's, but it's almost a symbiotic working relationship. And Panic wasn't in disagreement about this. Panic agreed that the Chief of Staff plays a big role, a very important role, a very close role with the commander. But apart from being just the Chief of Staff, if I can say that, we have to consider his role that day and his awareness of the prisoners' situation. Because here we have not just a Chief of Staff but one who was highly engaged in his commander's activities on the 20th of November concerning the prisoners. Now, don't forget, Mrksic had sent Panic to be his representative to the government meeting. So he trusted Panic to go and convey his agreement with the government's decision to take over the prisoners. They spoke before Panic went to the meeting, they spoke after he got out of the meeting, Panic all the while keeping Mrksic updated about basically what was going on with the prisoners and the government's decision. And then he goes off to Ovcara so he can go and make a report to Mrksic. They're actively involved together about the prisoners at this stage. And he went and told Mrksic what he'd seen, although he gave a rather sanitised account about that. The third fact that we have to bear in mind is that he was taking over as acting commander the next day, and also considering the importance of the decision to withdraw the security from Ovcara. And in light of the time we will detail this more in our submissions, but essentially it's simply not believable that Mrksic kept his Chief of Staff out of the loop on this order. Now, even more inconceivable, Your Honours, is his claim that he did not learn of the withdrawal order or anything about its terrible consequences until he returned to Belgrade several days later, four days later. So the implication is that he thought that the prisoners of war were at Ovcara being guarded by the 80th Brigade, if you accept his version. Yet, despite taking over as acting commander on the 21st and 22nd of November, he failed to take any steps whatsoever to even acquaint himself with their situation or take steps to follow up. And this has to be seen -- questioned in light of his previous concern for the prisoners the day before. And in our submission, the only reason for this incoherence is that he knew the true state of affairs and was determined to isolate himself as much as possible from it. Now, I've mentioned from the 21st of November until Mrksic returned on the 22nd of November, Panic was acting commander of the OG South. And we heard today from Mr. Theunens that that position carries with it the duty to keep aware of the situation in the units over which he's commanding. He was obliged to seek out information about his units and what they were doing. He was obliged to seek out information about the prisoners under guard by the OG South units. And as Mr. Theunens explained, this isn't like a passive duty where you sort of wait around and hope the information sort of comes your way, it's not a passive duty; it's a very active duty. He has to ensure a constant monitoring of data, monitoring of the situation, so he can issue prompt decisions and orders and so thereby make prompt and timely reports to his superiors. So upon assuming command of OG South on the 21st, military doctrine dictates that Panic should have kept himself apprised of the situation. If he didn't get reports from the 80th, he was duty-bound to go and get them, either personally or he could send somebody, especially given his concerns the previous day. In our submission, the fact he did nothing at all speaks volumes. And the reason why is that he knew the true state of affairs and he was distancing himself from it. Now, I want to turn to three I guess key reasons, the three main reasons why -- which Panic gives as to why he did nothing to follow-up on the prisoners, nothing, not a word about these prisoners that he's so concerned with before. Each one of his explanations is -- so defies key tenets of military doctrine that these lies should cause you to have serious doubts about his credibility. First, he suggested, and Judge Meron asked me -- Judge Meron asked me to point to the transcript where Panic had said this. He suggested -- well, he actually said it, that the 80th Motorised Brigade had sole responsibility for the Ovcara area and had ceased to be the subordinate to the OG South by the 21st of November. This is completely false and it runs directly counter to the principle of single authority and unity of command. What he's trying to imply is that from the 20th/21st of November, the 80th already had sole responsibility for Ovcara, even though the Trial Chamber itself already found that the OG South was -- retained responsibility for all subordinate units within its zone including the 80th until the 23rd of November. These are the Trial Chamber's findings at 82 and 253. Now, it's true, the 80th Brigade was going to take over when the Guards departed, but until that - and we heard this today from Mr. Theunens and it's very much part of his report - according to that principle of single authority and unity of command, only one unit can be in charge at one time and that was OG South. So while the preparations for the take-over by the 80th of the OG South zone was a gradual process and taking place over several days, the actual transfer of authority took place at a specific moment in time and that was after the 23rd of November, 6.00 p.m., and before 24th of November when they left. And until that point the OG South commander retains responsibility, overall responsibility, for the situation in that zone of responsibility. And we can see this clearly from the orders that were issued by both Mrksic and Panic to the 80th Motorised Brigade in the period 21 to 23 November. These are Exhibits 422 and 424. If the 80th were not still being subordinate, were not then subordinate to the OG South, why are they being issued orders. The second reason -- I'm sorry, I realised, Your Honours, that I'm actually now at the 30 minutes. If I could ask for your indulgence, I should be able to complete my submissions in about five more minutes, seven minutes maximum. The second reason Mr. Panic gave why he showed no concern, no follow-up to the prisoners when he was acting commander is he says in effect that he was command in a formal sense only. And by this I mean -- we refer to his testimony at the pre-review hearing, page 71, you will recall he said this: "Mrksic was still alive. He was right there. He had communications equipment and was soon back from Belgrade." And he also left open the possibility and it was explored today in questioning of Mr. Theunens, not with much effect I would add, but that he claimed he didn't communicate with the 80th command on the morning of the 21st, but he suggested that Mrksic may have. He said "perhaps by phone," and that's at page 71. Well, we heard what Mr. Theunens said about that in answer to Judge Pocar's question, that essentially if Mrksic had rung up and told an operations officer, the operations officer would have gone to Mr. Panic who was then acting commander, otherwise there's complete chaos and that's the whole idea of singleness of authority and unity of command. Basically, this is another example of Panic misleading this Chamber. It defies core -- you know, this core principle of single authority to suggest that he was not fully in command that day, but somehow Mrksic was pulling the strings from outside and actively commanding and receiving operational reports to Panic's exclusion. Well, if that in itself contradicts Exhibit 368, which is the regular combat report which he signed which he sent to his superiors in the 1 MD, signed as acting commander on the 21st of November at 6.00 p.m., where he's covering all the situational developments in the preceding 24 hours. The last explanation Mr. Panic gave for why he wouldn't have followed up with the prisoners is that basically he said he was too busy attending to other tasks, all these other things that he had that day, like the press conference, the return of the Guards to Belgrade, and taking care of civilian convoys. This is an astonishing statement. It runs completely counter to his duty as acting commander to remain aware of what the units under his command are doing, not to mention prisoners of war who were being guarded by them. And as Mr. Theunens has explained, the number and nature of tasks that a commander has at any one given time doesn't impact on the duties that he has under this SFRY or armed forces doctrine, very basic points of military doctrine. He has to keep aware of the situation of his units and the prisoners of war, not just so he knows what to do himself but he's also got this obligation going up to his superiors. So he can't just say, "Oh, well, you know, I was too busy." If need be, he's got to prioritise, he's got to delegate his tasks. In our submission, if he was truly so preoccupied with other tasks, this was a deliberate choice by him to remain purposely ignorant. One final remark, Your Honours, before I conclude. When you come to assess Panic's credibility, I ask you to look closely at Exhibit 368, this report that he signed as acting commander and sent to his superiors at 6.00 p.m. on the 21st of November. And don't forget what this is, it's a report to his superiors about the preceding 24 hours in Vukovar. So by necessity it should have mentioned the main activities in that period by OG South units, which would, by necessity, include information about 200 prisoners of war that they'd got and, you know, the fact that the 80th Motorised Brigade was with them. Well, what does it record about those topics when we have a look at that report? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. It does mention the transfer of the civilians and it does mention the transfer of the wounded and the sick in the previous 24 hours, but absolutely no mention at all of the transfer of 200 prisoners of war to the government or even -- or to Ovcara. They have simply vanished, vanished from the radar, not in his report. The exclusion of any information whatsoever about the prisoners from this 21st of November report was Panic's deliberate attempt to isolate himself from the situation at Ovcara, just as he has done whenever he testifies about these matters including in these review proceedings. In conclusion, Your Honours, Panic cannot be believed about the conversation. On this issue his self-interest and his bias is palpable. His professed ignorance of the withdrawal order that evening and the following four days, despite being Chief of Staff, despite being acting commander, is implausible in light of military doctrine and the operational context. That being so, his testimony, what he's told you about the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin, has no impact on Sljivancanin's conviction. And those conclude my submissions. I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. I note that you use now in concluding the word "implausible" which appeared throughout the report of your expert. At one point today at least you upgraded that word a little bit to "inconceivable." I did ask Mr. Theunens whether implausible means impossible and you know that he was not prepared to make a commitment on that. And things happen in the fog of war and we must be very careful about very serious matters like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And you rightly pointed out that the question of credibility of Colonel Panic is very central to this review. And I trust that in your summary submissions you will identify -- try to identify any discrepancies between Mr. -- Colonel Panic's testimony and prior statements or anything else relevant to the question of his credibility and of course Mr. Bourgon will have six days after that so he will have ample time and space to answer this. Do I see any questions? I do not. So we will now move -- I'm terribly sorry. Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask Ms. Brady the following. Is it really possible for someone who is not prosecuted by the Prosecutor, someone like Mr. Panic -- just the fact of coming to testify in favour of someone, here it's Mr. Sljivancanin. Does this mean that he absolutely has to defend him in order to protect himself? Is it automatic according to you or do you think that someone can just -- can't someone just come to say the truth must be told and I will testify to the truth without trying to protect this person, especially since this person is not being prosecuted at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right, Your Honour. It is possible someone could come and say, "Well, no, I want to have the truth be told and this is what it is" without himself being guilty -- without himself actually being guilt. But in our submission if you put all the facts that we've outlined, and our submissions will make it clearer, together you get a picture, and taking into account the Trial Chamber 's findings about his credibility where they treated it with rather a large grain of salt, we are submitting that you should also treat his evidence with a large grain of salt that, yes, somebody could come along and just tell the truth. You don't mean to say you're biassed for that person or you're protecting yourself, but in light of all the facts, in light of the military doctrine which was sort of out the window completely, thrown out the window, none of this was working that day, frankly when you add up all these details it does not add up in our submission. And the real reason why he came to give evidence is a combination of self-interest. Yes, I know he wasn't actually prosecuted, but that doesn't mean that he's not potentially in a difficult situation, in a tight situation, himself in other countries or in other jurisdictions. He doesn't have to be an accused himself to have self-interest. In our submission, he's so close to these events and that in itself would cause you to have a serious doubt when seen in light of everything else that he's testified about. And the clear three lies, the foundational lies that I've pointed out to -- I think in my submission establish that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I believe that Judge Pocar has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was just wondering whether it is your position -- we heard that Panic spontaneously went, if I'm correct, to the Defence team after he heard that Sljivancanin had been convicted. Is that correct? My recollection is correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now, is that your point that he did so because the judgement of the Trial Chamber as referred to by the Appeals Chamber mentioned that -- or claim to the conclusion that Mrksic told or must have told Sljivancanin during that conversation to which Panic was present, was attending that conversation. So if Mrksic had told Sljivancanin on that occasion that the order had been given, Panic would have heard of the order because he was present. So he -- it's your point that for your position that he came up with the -- to the Defence trying to protect himself against a possible prosecution based on the fact that it was -- that he knew of the order according to the conclusions of the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Of course you mentioned yourself he would not be subject to any prosecution before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Because the prosecutions are closed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Right, right but they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But he may be before a domestic court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: But Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I was wondering if it was your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, firstly I think you need to say that it's not just a question of is he going to be prosecuted, but also how it looks to the outside world when this finding is left hanging, as it were, in the appeals judgement. So when he finds out -- he told us that when he found out that Sljivancanin was convicted he said, "Oh, you know, what's the basis?" And we recall that he asked his daughter to help him with the translation and he quickly looked at that. It's very difficult. I would be in the land of speculation if I said, "Well, it's definitely for this reason that he got up out of his house and charged over and contacted Mr. Lukic." Of course we can't say that, but what we can say is that he has several very powerful incentives to come up with this story, to help Sljivancanin, to continue to protect the Guards Brigade, to protect himself. Any one or more the combination of those reasons could have led him to finally decide: Yes, great, I'm going to go and contact Mr. Lukic. But apart from that, I would be speculating, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think that we will now move on to Mr. Bourgon for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, honourable Judges, as I begin this oral submission which is so important for Mr. Sljivancanin, I will begin simply by recalling why is it that we are here today. In other words, we need to remind ourselves of the exceptional circumstances of this case. What are the exceptional circumstances of this case? Well, you have an officer who has been convicted for aiding and abetting by omission a number of prisoners of war which is a very severe conviction. The gravity can certainly not be undermined. But how did this conviction come about? This conviction come about of something that was not anticipated initially, whether at trial or even on appeal. It wasn't even a ground of appeal. It did become a ground of appeal or not a ground of appeal -- it did draw the interests of the Appeals Chamber in extremis, on the basis of what the Appeals Chamber found in paragraph 62 of its judgement. And what did the Appeals Chamber find? They say the only possible conclusion or reasonable conclusion is that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the military police. And on this basis, this provided Sljivancanin with the necessary mens rea for aiding and abetting by omission and he was convicted. The issue here is that as soon as this conviction became public knowledge someone who was present during that specific conversation, a senior officer of the JNA, and this senior officer, a former very high-level commander, he said, "I was there. I know that Mrksic did not say that. And I must do something about it." Now, Mr. Theunens today did not want to agree with me that any senior officer would want to do that if he knows the truth. That's okay. You saw -- you saw Mr. Theunens how he reacted to my question and how defensive he was in trying to avoid answering the plain truth. Because of course I look at it from the opposite point of view as opposed to the Prosecution. They look at it from the point of view he came forward to protect himself. I submit to you, Mr. President, that he came to you to prevent an injustice. And that's the whole difference, complete difference, between the two positions. And this is the crux of the matter in this case. Everyone knew that Panic was there during that conversation. That was established by the Trial Chamber. The Appeals Chamber also referred to the Trial Chamber's conclusion in saying that Panic was there. But it was established in your decision, Mr. President, on 14 July that the fact that Panic heard this conversation and the fact that during this conversation Mrksic did not say that he had withdrawn the military police, that this was something new, that this was a new fact that could reverse the judgement. From that point on, all of our attention must be directed to one thing: Did Panic hear the conversation and did Mrksic say whether there was -- whether he had withdrawn the MPs. The Prosecution's position, they have not one iota of evidence in addition to what was already considered by the Trial Chamber and what was reviewed by the Appeals Chamber to say that Mrksic did say that he had withdrawn the military police during this conversation. So they say then we have no evidence. Panic must be a liar. That's all they got. I agree with you, Mr. President, it is a central issue, but before we go and we think and we make the step of thinking that someone can simply to avoid an absolutely hypothetical prosecution, hypothetical problems, to come and put himself before this Tribunal -- and having been there he testified here before, he worked before with all -- with the Defence team of Mrksic, he worked before with the Defence team of Sljivancanin, he gave a statement to the Prosecution, he testified here for four days, he was examined, cross-examined by three different parties, asked questions to the Judges. Even if someone did not have anything to hide, they would say: I'm not going to go back there again. But him, yes, he will go back there. So the key question with respect to the credibility is exactly this: Did he try to protect himself? Did he do this in order to shield some possible responsibility? And my question -- my response to this answer is a clear no. Now, we look at the conversation itself and that's what we have to focus on. The conversation itself, we say how could the Prosecution say or show that what Panic says is not true? Well, there are many things which the Prosecution could have done to find evidence. What is more, they did it. We all know that they investigated this case to the limit. When the Prosecution filed its motion for extension of time, that was I believe on 22 July, they said, "Well, we looked at Panic's testimony and we have lots of witnesses that we identified that we want to speak to. And we also have filed a request for assistance to this government and a request for assistance to that government. It is evident that they were going out of their way to find something in order to show that this was not the truth. What'd they come up with? An expert witness who says that because SFRY doctrine was not applied, Panic is a liar. Of course it's a bit of a jump what I'm saying here, but it remains the fact. All they can come up with is an expert witness who's going to say SFRY doctrine was not applied, so these actions are not plausible. But the Trial Chamber looked at the doctrine, had the opportunity of hearing expert witnesses on the doctrine, and they made some pretty good findings on the doctrine, saying the doctrine was not being applied consistently, the doctrine was not being adhered to. But not only in the creation of Operational Group South but also in the chain of command. So now we have to look again. I look at Mrksic because the expert says and I guess the Prosecution would like us to believe that, that Mrksic -- it's not possible that Mrksic did not give the order without telling Panic. Okay. Well, let's look at that. Of course the expert will never want to say that there are such possibilities. But when a man commits a crime - and that's what Mrksic did at that time, he was committing a crime. So he's committing a crime and this expert who's never been to war, who's never been a Chief of Staff, who's never been into any operational environment, is going to go on and say: Oh, yes, he had to tell the Chief of Staff, of course. Mr. President, we can't bring any weight to such statement. He didn't even want to put his money where his mouth is, as we say, and say that it's impossible. He agrees that it was possible. Let's take a look, Mr. President, at what the Prosecution could have done and most likely did in order to look for evidence. Because if Panic lied about the conversation, there are many people who could have been interviewed again to give us some idea that Panic knew of the order in the evening of 20 November 1991 and there is also a number of people who could have been interviewed to know that during the period from 21 November until 24 November, Panic somehow did get the information that a crime had been committed. And if he did, that's why he obtained information on the 23rd that may possibly bring his liability, so he's going to lie about a conversation in the evening of 20 November. He will take the risk to come here, to get into this environment, and to testify that it was not mentioned in the evening of 20 November because he wants to avoid the fact and hide the fact that he learned later on. The Prosecution could have interviewed the persons in the command of Operational Group South. They must have done it. No evidence. The Prosecution could have interviewed witnesses who were with Panic during those days. They must have done it. No evidence. Not one who can come and say: I know that Panic was aware, not one. That's the key, Mr. President. They could have interviewed witnesses who were present at any event attended by Panic to find someone who could say that he was made aware. Now, this applies to witnesses who already testified and it applies to new witnesses, and new witnesses would have been admitted at this hearing to come and say that Panic was aware, that Panic really did not do something knowing that this was the case. Nope, nothing, not one. But I'm sure that the Office of the Prosecution did investigate. Let's take one example, Mr. President. There was - and I'm looking now to 21 November because the Prosecution focused most of its cross-examination -- of its examination-in-chief today to the 21 of November, that appears to be their -- main thrust of their theory, that he learned later on and because of that he comes and lies about the 20th because he learned on the 22nd. On the 21st Panic was at a press briefing. There were at this press briefing, according to the evidence we have, 120 or more people from the media, both national and international. If there had been rumours about what happened to the prisoners, one of these people from the media would have picked that up. If it was so much known, it would have been picked up somehow by somebody. No. The only people who talked about this order are those who were involved. The evidence in this case shows, if you look at the evidence, you have the colonel of 80th Motorised Brigade, he was giving the order; you have Karanfilov, he denied receiving the order; you have Vukosavljevic, he was given the order to transmit; you have Vezmarovic, he was the guy who executed the order; and you have P14, the guy who was right beside Ovcara, less than 200 metres away and who discusses the issue with Mrksic; you also have the Chief of Staff of 80th Motorised Brigade, Danilovic, he testified, he was cross-examined. Those people became in possession of the order but no one else. There's a reason for that. There's a reason why Mrksic did not tell Panic. There's a reason why Vojnovic did not tell anybody. And there's a reason why it did not get out of this close circle. And there's no evidence that this information ever reached Miodrag Panic. That's the key to this information. Let us look at what the expert said today because we think that this is nothing but relitigation. That's been our view. We put it on paper and we say it again today. The expert, I asked him a few questions about the evidence; he wasn't even aware of it. Some key findings quite closely related to the issue at hand, he did not look. Of course he looked at the paragraphs that the Prosecution gave him. That's normal. He's a former OTP Prosecutor -- or Prosecutor is not the right word but analyst working for the Prosecution. If we think of bias in this case, Mr. President, it's certainly not Panic who's biassed; it's this guy who comes and sits here and plays the game with the Prosecution. At least if they could bring forward a real general, someone who's been there. They must have found one -- I mean, I know it's different, I have access to lots of those before somebody says that, but they could have brought a real general, they could have brought somebody with operational experience. The way he answered the question to Judge Pocar -- I mean, I'm not going to take the time to get -- to lead further evidence to show that it's simply not correct, but I will argue to you that it is simply not correct. It is not true that the commander of the 80th Brigade getting an order from Mrksic who is in Belgrade is going to say, well, comrade Mrksic wait a minute, I need to check with Panic before I take your order. This is simply not the way it works. Where does this guy come from? I don't know. And when a question is put to him, what's more important? Is it more important to look at the prisoners or to look at other operational requirements? How could he ever know? He's never been a Chief of Staff. The book will not be of any assistance in saying that. He might have conducted interviews with generals. I too. Could I give you a real solid opinion as to what is the choice to be made by someone in such difficult circumstances? I could not. And I put it to you that he cannot either and which shows that everything that he said must be completely disregarded because that's not the issue. The issue in this case is the evidence and nothing but the evidence. But the fact that the Prosecution -- sorry, the Trial Chamber has looked at all these events. When I look at the evidence I say: Okay, let's see what we got to show that Panic was aware before the conversation, before the conversation. I asked this -- the expert, Mr. Theunens, I asked him -- of course you know that it was not mentioned at the briefing. Now, is it the Prosecution's case that it was? Well, then we have to relitigate and call all these witnesses again. We'll have to call Gluscevic, Lesanovic, Trifunovic, who else? Because it's clear from the evidence that this was never mentioned at the judgement -- sorry, at the daily briefing. If it's not mentioned at the daily briefing, what possibility -- what timing is left between the daily briefing and the conversation with Sljivancanin? Very little time. What happens during that very little time? Well, we know that during that time Mrksic has the conversation with Vojnovic and with Vukosavljevic and that this conversation takes place outside. Was Panic privy to that conversation in any way based on the evidence? No. Did the Prosecution bring a witness to say that Panic was close to that conversation? No. Why did the Prosecution not call Vojnovic back here? He's the one who failed to report the order. He's the one who did -- executed an illegal order. He's the one who told the next day according to the evidence he told all his officers: Make sure you tell everybody that this shall not happen again. He's the one who told P14, and he was surprised when P14 told him the people -- there are rumours -- that there are rumours that the prisoners were murdered. And this guy, he should be here to testify and to tell the Appeals Chamber: I know that Panic knows, but he's not here to do that. Why did they not call him back? Why not call back Vukosavljevic and see maybe Panic heard or he was at the end of the room. The reason is simple: They're not coming because Panic was not aware of that conversation. Not only it's not in the evidence, they can't find more evidence that it was. So now we're in the middle of the conversation. We covered before because Panic said that he did not see Karanfilov at the command and the Prosecution did nothing about that. And then we say the daily briefing, that's covered. The period between the daily briefing and the conversation, that's covered. The conversation itself, we have no other evidence. We are left with nothing, Mr. President. We're left with simply the Prosecution's theory that someone lied because he learned later -- because he must have learned. The stakes are too high to jump into that -- to make that jump, way too high. What matters is the evidence, not whether doctrine was applied. Because -- especially about the doctrine, it's important to recall that when this -- the expert -- he says Mrksic should have told Panic. Panic says yes. He says Panic should have reacted when he was told. Panic says: If I had been told I would have reacted. So where is the line? The Prosecution would like to give you three examples where apparently Panic misled or misguided or lied before the Trial Chamber. Well, there's two issues here: One, all those three issues that they relate to have nothing to do with responsibility, but I don't have time to do this right now. This will be later. But the key issue - and I was -- I did not know that Mr. Theunens was present when Mr. Panic was interviewed. Now we know, he was there. At trial in his statement and at trial Panic said: I don't know who issued the order. I know Mrksic, he's not the type to issue such an order, but it can only come from the commander. Biassed you say? He got his commander convicted and he's biassed? Biassed for Sljivancanin? Where's the evidence? Where's the evidence that he biassed? There's no bias here. He convicted the commander of the Operational Group South. Can you imagine how difficult that must have been for Mr. Panic to do that. And he said no order. And the Prosecution, they took this information, they liked what he said because he said that it can only come from Mrksic, so they grabbed the ball and they ran with the ball and they ran as quick as they can -- as they could and they got a conviction against Mrksic. You want to challenge Panic? Hey listen, it's not possible that you did not know that. Come on. Don't pull a fast one like us. We're going to look like fools in the evidence if you say that. Don't do that to us. That's not possible. I mean, Theunens was there, that was the time to say: Mr. Panic, you're the Chief of Staff, it's not possible that you don't know. Did he say that? Did the Prosecution do anything at that time? No. But now, oh, now it's different. Now it's different because he's saying the truth again but this time they don't like it because they might have a conviction overturned. So suddenly Panic becomes not credible and they will do everything to ensure that the world knows that Panic is a bad officer. Well, I hope, Mr. President, that this will not be the case in whatever judgement you render about the qualities of Panic who came here to testify. I have four minutes left. I will do one more -- one last thing I wish to say and that's the following, which is of course -- again I come back to the conversation because we really believe that this is the crux of the matter, not after, not before, it's the conversation. We already said if Mrksic is committing a criminal act he's not likely to tell Sljivancanin. I mean, this theme of being scared of security officers is a recurring theme in many trials before this Tribunal. Now, the expert would like you -- would like you to believe that because of Article 36 of the Law on the Applicability of International Laws of War, because under law I commit a crime and I'm going to turn myself in, I'm going to tell Sljivancanin I committed a crime. And then, Mr. President, the same goes for Karanfilov. Why would Mrksic tell Sljivancanin, oh, by the way, Sljivancanin I told Karanfilov to remove the MPs. It makes no sense. And my last thing, Mr. President, is you've seen Panic testify. He's not the type of guy, unlike my friend Sljivancanin who likes the media and who likes the highlight, and who's paying a big price because he liked the media in 1991. You saw Panic, very reserved, you saw his character, you saw how he testified, you saw him respond to your questions. And on all the -- on the basis of what you saw and on the basis of the evidence on the record and on the basis of the fact that there is no additional evidence pointing to the contrary, we respectfully ask you, Mr. President, to recognise that what Panic came to say before this Tribunal has been proved and accordingly that the conviction of Sljivancanin for aiding and abetting murder by omission must be overturned. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. These proceedings are now coming to a close. I remind the parties that pursuant to our order entitled: "Decision of the Admission of Evidence and Scheduling Order," the parties are ordered to file written submissions following today's hearing. The Prosecution has been granted seven days following the review hearing to file its submission. And counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will then have seven days from the date of the Prosecution's filing to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The Prosecution is then given a further four days from the date of Mr. Sljivancanin's filing to reply. Before concluding, I want to consult the Bench about something, so you will bear with me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you are about to consult about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Not about -- please give me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you maybe -- because we are -- we would like to address you concerning a number of pages in those submissions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Bourgon. I did not forget you. You want to make a statement or say something about the number of pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You -- the norm is 3.000 normally in these things, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That would be perfectly fine with us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So this resolves the problem. Is this a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It is a problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It is a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It is a problem because we need more words than 3.000 to put all the evidence to make all the links. It's a complicated matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So what do you need, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: We would be asking for 15.000 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, that does not sound --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: That's approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That does not sound reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- 35 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: 15.000 instead of 3.000?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a number of different matters we have to go into and we have exhibits. We want to show you precisely where the inconsistencies where occurred. I mean, I'm in your hands, Your Honours, but we certainly need more than 3.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me first hear what Mr. Bourgon has to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are two issues here on behalf of the applicant. The first issue of course is that this is -- we are now briefing in writing after oral arguments. So everything has been heard already. We -- parties should be able to summarise their arguments, and for us a 3.000-word limit is perfectly fine. The second issue, Mr. President, is one of time and resources. Both Mr. Lukic and myself, we are both on other cases and we do not have the resources that are available to the Office of the Prosecution, whether in time or real resources. We would like and we believe that it is sufficient to maintain the 3.000 words. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will consult my colleagues -- yes, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: If I could just make one further comment on the word limit. Because 3.000 words, Your Honours, applies to motions. And here we're talking about something far more complicated. It's a review of an appeals judgement. Too much -- as my friend has said, too much rides on it to say, you know, put it in 3.000 words. That's ten pages, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will consult my colleagues and try to issue a ruling right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. The Bench will now rule with its own symbiotic judgement which is 4.000 words. Now, before concluding I would like to ask whether Mr. Sljivancanin would like to make a five-minute statement. It's -- you're certainly not obliged to do it, Major Sljivancanin. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen of the courtroom, I have spoken a lot in this trial. There has been no session when I didn't speak. I have come here to speak the truth and for nine days I have been examined by various Prosecutors and I have spoken the truth. I'm worried by the fact that honourable people are being attacked. Mr. Panic has never been a friend of mine and he associated more with other people than me. I'm sure that he spoke the truth and nothing but the truth, and I'm sorry for all the victims and I'm sorry that I lost my country which was Yugoslavia and that people had to die in those wars. I'm having a difficult time and I -- but I'm sure that the Judges will pass a -- the correct decision on behalf of all the future generations and for all the people who stand for truth and justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Sljivancanin. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have consulted the Bench on another aspect. I think that in my sort of conclusions I have suggested that the Prosecution would go first. I think it's more correct that Mr. Sljivancanin, who has submitted the appeal, should go first with the 4.000 words and be replied by the Prosecution. And I think that this will be it. Is there any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Who wants to go first? We have no problem with that change of order. It makes sense to us to put it in that order, given that the Defence bears the burden of showing how the new fact impacts on the conviction, so we would be happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No difficulty, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is -- we're the applicant. As long as we get to reply to reply. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I draw the attention of the parties that in the ruling that we now gave about the 4.000 and the order of submissions and this being it, basically we have somewhat diverted from the written order, Scheduling Order we have issued, but we think that in the circumstances of this rather exceptional case on review this may be a simpler way of proceeding. And I see no objections, and so it will be. So if I hear no additional comments from the parties or from my colleagues, the Court will now rise and we will await your submissions and work diligently on our decision. Thank you.
